title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
我
聖祖高皇帝臨御之初立賢無方
自洪武三年至五年每歲皆
開科取士既而謂所舉未足
以盡得人六年以後姑罷之
越十有一年為洪武甲子始
===
復
詔禮部與儒臣重議定科舉成
式頒行天下永為遵守今四
仲與四季年鄉試會試之制
是也則其法比前加密而取
士之道視唐宋以来科舉之
制尤盡善矣

會試錄序
我

復
詔禮部與儒臣重議定科舉成
式頒行天下永爲遵守令四
仲與四季年鄉試會試之制
是也則其法比前加密而取
士之道視唐宋以來科舉之
制尤盡善矣
punctuated:
會試錄序

我聖祖高皇帝臨御之初，立賢無方。自洪武三年至五年，每歲皆開科取士。既而謂所舉未足以盡得人，六年以後姑罷之。越十有一年，為洪武甲子，始復詔禮部與儒臣重議，定科舉成式，頒行天下，永為遵守。今四仲與四季年鄉試、會試之制是也。則其法比前加密，而取士之道，視唐宋以来科舉之制，尤盡善矣。
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

At the beginning of his reign, our Sacred Progenitor, Emperor Gao, appointed worthy men without restriction as to their source. From the third through the fifth year of Hongwu, examinations were held annually to select men for office. Subsequently, he judged that those recommended through the examinations did not adequately encompass all available talent, and from the sixth year onward he suspended them for the time being. Eleven years later, in the jiazi year of Hongwu [1384], he again issued an edict directing the Ministry of Rites and Confucian court officials to reconsider the matter together. They established a standard system for the civil-service examinations, promulgated it throughout the empire, and made it binding in perpetuity. This is the present system of holding the Provincial and Metropolitan Examinations respectively in the four middle and four final years of the twelve-year cycle. Its regulations were thus more thorough than before, and its method of selecting men for office was still more fully perfected than the examination systems of the Tang and Song dynasties and subsequent times.

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:

translation_en: Your servants Li Xunxue and Wu Yan, as the date of the Metropolitan Examination drew near, admonished their subordinates in advance, each to attend carefully to his duties without negligence. On the jihai day of the second month, your servant Xunxue, Director of the Examination, together with your servants Ping Shiyong and Wang Ci, the censors overseeing the examination, and the others, first took leave of Your Majesty and entered the examination compound to perform their duties with heightened care. Two days later, on the xinchou day, your servant Chu and Academician Mao Cheng had respectfully received the command to serve as Examiners, while Right Mentor Li Tingxiang; Compilers Huang Lan, Li Shi, Zhao Yong, Zhai Luan, Jing Yang, Yu Ben, Xu Chengming, Zhang Bi, and Zhang Chao; Examining Editor Sun Shaoxian; Left Supervising Secretary Zhang Yun; Supervising Secretaries Gao Fang and Wang Kuang; and Acting Vice Director Huang Gong …

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
臣陳槐主事臣夏良勝等亦
均有同考試之責又相與
陛辭入院涖事于簾內益加慎
焉盖自三試既畢硃卷續入
之後臣等各鞠躬盡瘁夜以
繼日惟恐簡閱或不當無以
稱
===
上意旨及乎簡閱既久甄别既明
於三千八百餘卷中奉
宸斷取其文之中式者四百人第
其姓名列為正榜又擇其文
之明暢者二十篇刻之試錄
將以進呈
乙覽而傳之于四方遠邇以昭

punctuated: 臣陳槐、主事臣夏良勝等，亦均有同考試之責，又相與陛辭，入院涖事于簾內，益加慎焉。盖自三試既畢、硃卷續入之後，臣等各鞠躬盡瘁，夜以繼日，惟恐簡閱或不當，無以稱上意旨。及乎簡閱既久，甄别既明，於三千八百餘卷中，奉宸斷取其文之中式者四百人，第其姓名，列為正榜。又擇其文之明暢者二十篇，刻之試錄，將以進呈乙覽，而傳之于四方遠邇，以昭
translation_en: …your servant Chen Huai, Secretary Xia Liangsheng, and the others likewise all bore responsibility as Associate Examiners. Together we took leave of Your Majesty and entered the examination compound to perform our duties within the curtain, exercising still greater care. After all three sessions had concluded and the vermilion copies of the examination papers began arriving in succession, we servants each devoted ourselves unstintingly to the task, working day and night. Our sole fear was that our scrutiny might be unsound and thus fail to accord with Your Majesty’s intentions. After prolonged scrutiny, once the distinctions among the papers were clear, we acted under Your Majesty’s judgment to select, from more than 3,800 papers, four hundred candidates whose compositions met the standard. We ranked their names and entered them on the principal list of successful candidates. We further selected twenty compositions distinguished by clarity and fluency and had them engraved for printing in the examination record, intending to submit it for Your Majesty’s perusal and circulate it throughout the land, near and far, to make manifest…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
科目盛事凡姓名之見錄于
此者亦云榮且遇矣况旬日
間又將入覲
大廷對揚
清問登科釋褐馴有官守言責
之寄他日之都高官任大事
為
國家建無窮勳業其本皆肇於
此不知諸士子平日之所以
抱負與他日之所以施為圖
報者其果皆能為麟為鳳以
瑞世為雨為露以潤物為楩
楠松栢以成大廈為桑麻菽
粟以濟人利物用求無媿于
alt_text:
科目盛事凡姓名之見錄于
此者亦云榮且遇矣況旬日
間又将入覲
大廷對揚
清問登科釋褐剬有官守言責
之寄他日之都高官任大事
為
===
國家建無窮勲業其本皆肇於
此不知諸士子平日之所以
抱負與他日之所以施為圖
報者其果皆能為麟為鳳以
瑞世為雨為露以潤物為楩
柟杉栢以成大厦為桑麻菽
粟以濟人利物用求無愧于
punctuated: 科目盛事。凡姓名之見錄于此者，亦云榮且遇矣。况旬日間，又將入覲大廷，對揚清問，登科釋褐，馴有官守言責之寄。他日之都高官、任大事，為國家建無窮勳業，其本皆肇於此。不知諸士子平日之所以抱負，與他日之所以施為圖報者，其果皆能為麟為鳳以瑞世，為雨為露以潤物，為楩楠松栢以成大廈，為桑麻菽粟以濟人利物，用求無媿于
translation_en: …the grand occasion of the examinations. All whose names are recorded here may indeed be said to have gained honor and enjoyed a fortunate opportunity. Moreover, within ten days they will enter the great court for an imperial audience and respond to His Majesty’s searching questions. They will attain examination rank, put aside commoners’ dress, and in due course be entrusted with official duties and responsibilities of remonstrance. Their future attainment of high office, assumption of great responsibilities, and establishment of enduring achievements for the state all have their beginnings here. I wonder whether the aspirations these scholars have long cherished, and the deeds through which they will seek to repay imperial favor in the future, will indeed enable them all to become qilin and phoenixes, bringing auspicious blessings to the age; rain and dew, nourishing all things; pian and nan timber trees, pines and cypresses, furnishing the materials for a great edifice; and mulberry, hemp, beans, and grain, sustaining people and benefiting all things—thereby seeking to be worthy of …

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
科目且無負於
國家培養
恩德否乎有則請為諸士子喜
之幸之且屬望之不然則非
爾主司之所知也亦非我
國家今日之所以求賢之意也
烏乎諸士子其尚勉之哉
===
光祿大夫柱國少傅兼太
子太傅吏部尚書
謹身殿大學士梁儲謹序
alt_text:
科目且無負於
國家培養
恩德否乎有則請為諸士子喜
之幸之且屬望之不然則非
爾主司之所知也亦非我
國家今日之所以求賢之意也
烏乎諸士子其尚勉之哉
===
光祿大夫柱國少傅兼太
子太傅吏部尚書
謹身殿大學士袁煒謹序
punctuated:
科目，且無負於國家培養恩德否乎？有則請為諸士子喜之、幸之，且屬望之；不然，則非爾主司之所知也，亦非我國家今日之所以求賢之意也。烏乎！諸士子其尚勉之哉！

光祿大夫、柱國、少傅兼太子太傅、吏部尚書、謹身殿大學士梁儲謹序。
translation_en:
…the examination system, and not disappoint the state's gracious care in nurturing them? If so, let me rejoice for these candidates, count them fortunate, and place my hopes in them. Otherwise, this falls outside what your examiners can countenance, and is likewise contrary to our state's purpose in seeking worthy men today. Ah! May all you candidates exert yourselves!

Respectfully composed as a preface by Liang Chu 梁儲, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Preceptor and concurrently Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Hall of Scrupulous Conduct.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Ninth Year of Zhengde (1514).

Officials in Charge of the Examination:

Liu Chun, Grand Master for Assisting Goodness and Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Renzhong and was from Ba County, Sichuan. He became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the dingwei year (1487).

Li Xunxue, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Xixian and was from Shangcai County, Henan. He became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1487).

Examiners:

Liang Chu, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Mentor concurrently serving as Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Jinshen Hall, had the courtesy name Shuhou and was from Shunde County, Guangdong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the wuxu year (1478).

Mao Cheng, Academician of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Governance, had the courtesy name Xianqing and was from Taicang Subprefecture in the directly administered territory. He became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1493).

Associate Examiners:

Li Tingxiang, Right Companion of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently serving as Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Mengbi and was from Pu Subprefecture, Shandong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1502).

Huang Lan, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Yuanxu and was from Putian County, Fujian. He became a metropolitan graduate in the guichou year (1493).

Li Shi, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Scholarly Service, had the courtesy name Zongyi and was from Renqiu County in the directly administered territory. He became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1502).

Zhao Yong, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Scholarly Service, had the courtesy name Erxi and was from Linhuai County in the directly administered territory. He became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1502).

Zhai Luan, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Scholarly Service, had the courtesy name Zhongming and belonged to the Embroidered-uniform Guard. He became a metropolitan graduate in the yichou year (1505).

Jing Yang, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Scholarly Service, had the courtesy name Boshi. He was registered in Shangyuan County, Yingtian Prefecture, and was a native of Yizhen County in the directly administered territory. He became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year (1508).

Yu Ben, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Zihua and was from Yin County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

第壹場

四書

欲誠其意者，先致其知；致知在格物。物格而后知至，知至而后意誠。

夫子之文章，可得而聞也；夫子之言性與天道，不可得而聞也。

於季桓子，見行可之仕也。

易

君子敬以直內，義以方外，敬義立而德不孤。

六四，樽酒簋貳，用缶，納約自牖，終无咎。

通其變，使民不倦；神而化之，使民宜之。易，窮則變，變則通，通則久。是以自天祐之，吉无不利。

六者非他也，三才之道也。

書

九功惟叙，九叙惟歌。戒之用休，董之用威，勸之以九歌，俾勿壞。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Those who wished to make their intentions sincere first extended their knowledge to the utmost. Extending knowledge lies in investigating things. Once things are investigated, knowledge reaches its utmost extent; once knowledge reaches its utmost extent, intentions become sincere.

The Master's cultural accomplishments can be heard about; his statements concerning human nature and the Way of Heaven cannot be heard.

In the case of Ji Huanzi, he took office because he saw that his Way could be put into practice.

Book of Changes

The noble man uses reverence to make his inner self upright and righteousness to make his outward conduct square. When reverence and righteousness are established, his virtue does not stand alone.

Six in the fourth place: a vessel of wine and two baskets of food, using earthenware vessels; presenting these simple offerings through the window. In the end, there is no blame.

Carry through the changes so that the people do not grow weary; transform things with wondrous efficacy so that the people find them fitting. In the Changes, reaching an extreme brings change; change brings free passage; free passage brings endurance. Thus, Heaven itself assists him: good fortune, with nothing unfavorable.

The six are nothing other than the Way of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humankind.

Book of Documents

When the nine achievements are duly ordered, celebrate their ordering in song. Admonish them with favorable words, supervise them with authority, and encourage them with the nine songs, so that these achievements do not fall into ruin.

translation_en:
…to secure the blessings of the former kings and forever establish the livelihood of the multitude.

To display King Wen’s radiant glory and proclaim King Wu’s great achievements.

The awe inspired by virtue alone is to be feared; the illumination of virtue alone truly enlightens. He therefore commanded the three lords to devote themselves to work for the people. Bo Yi promulgated the statutes, guiding the people by proper models; Yu regulated the waters and land and designated the principal mountains and rivers; Ji taught sowing and planting, cultivating fine grain. The three lords accomplished their work, bringing abundance to the people. The Minister of Justice regulated the hundred clans through a balanced application of punishments, teaching them to revere virtue. Majestic above and enlightened below, virtue shone throughout the four quarters, and all diligently pursued it. Thus, through an enlightened and balanced application of punishments, he guided and governed the people, supporting their constant moral nature.

Book of Odes

He seeks her but cannot obtain her; waking and sleeping, he thinks of her.

The multitudes of the common people everywhere follow your virtuous example.

Worthy men are a fence; the multitude is a wall. Great states are a screen; great lineages are supporting pillars. Cherishing virtue brings peace; the head of the royal lineage is a fortified city.

Model yourself upon and follow King Wen’s statutes, daily bringing peace to the four quarters. That great King Wen has already graciously accepted the offering.

Spring and Autumn Annals

The first year. 〔The first year of Duke Yin.〕 Autumn, the seventh month. 〔Also: the sixth year of Duke Yin.〕

The army encamped at Lang to await the men of Chen and Cai. 〔Also: the eighth year of Duke Zhuang.〕 The army of Qi …

Book of Rites
When virtue is perfected, instruction is honored; when instruction is honored, officials act correctly; when officials act correctly, the state is well governed.
When a disposition of ease, uprightness, kindness [?], and sincerity arises, there is joy. Joy brings peace; peace brings endurance; endurance brings accord with Heaven; accord with Heaven brings spiritual efficacy.
Thus the gentleman hears much, examines it, and holds fast to it; records much [?], examines it, and makes it his own; understands precisely, grasps the essentials, and puts them into practice.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven takes the full staffing of offices as his measure; the feudal lords take attending the Son of Heaven at the proper times as their measure; ministers and great officers take following the laws as their measure; servicemen take not neglecting their duties…

聖祖高皇帝在位餘三十年其

punctuated: 問：我聖祖高皇帝在位餘三十年，其嘉言善行、謨訓功烈，見於日曆之所紀載、史氏之所續書，與後來實錄之所纂修、五倫書之所表出者，明且詳矣。况舊章成憲，副在有司，丕顯丕承，萬代如見。諸士子之得於聞見者，盖亦深矣，亦能為我鋪張揚厲於萬一乎？抑聞聖祖之在當時，好古敏求，惟日不足。萬幾之暇，常好觀《洪範》《大誥》《無逸》《六典》《春秋》，及漢之詔令、唐之《帝範》，并《貞觀政要》、劉向《說苑》、《大學衍義》等書。不知當時御製諸不刊之典，及臣下奉㫖所撰次諸書，如《皇明祖訓》《三編大誥》《資世通訓》，及《皇明寶訓》《大明律令》《諸司職掌》《大明集禮》之類，亦有擬古而作，與《洪範》等書相表裏者乎？抑或但存之于
translation_en:
Question: Our Sagely Ancestor, Emperor Gao, reigned for more than thirty years. His exemplary words and good deeds, counsels and instructions, achievements and illustrious merits are clearly and fully set forth in the daily chronicles, in the historians’ successive accounts, in the Veritable Records compiled afterward, and in the Book of the Five Relationships. Moreover, copies of the established regulations and enacted statutes remain with the responsible offices, to be gloriously upheld and transmitted, as though present before the eyes of ten thousand generations. You examination candidates must also have gained a deep understanding through what you have heard and seen. Can you set forth and extol for us even one ten-thousandth of these accomplishments?
We have also heard that the Sagely Ancestor loved antiquity and diligently sought knowledge, finding each day insufficient. In the intervals between his myriad affairs of state, he regularly enjoyed reading the Great Plan, the Great Announcement, Against Idleness, the Six Statutes, and the Spring and Autumn Annals, as well as the edicts of the Han, the Tang work Model for Emperors, the Essentials of Government of the Zhenguan Reign, Liu Xiang’s Garden of Persuasions, and the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning, among other works. We wonder whether the enduring canonical works he composed at that time, together with the books his ministers compiled by imperial command—such as the Ancestral Instructions of the August Ming, the Three Compilations of the Great Announcements, the Comprehensive Instructions for Guiding the World, the Precious Instructions of the August Ming, the Laws and Ordinances of the Great Ming, the Duties of the Various Offices, and the Collected Rituals of the Great Ming—also included works modeled on antiquity that complemented the Great Plan and the other books. title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
聖心發之而為大訓行之而為大典有不專在
于言語文字間也主司於此固願有聞
焉
問自古賢聖之君不以天無災異為可喜
惟自以德政未修為可懼故古今論者
皆以為洪水九年而堯致治大旱七年
而湯修德桑穀生朝而太戊中興雉雊
鼎耳而武丁道盛漢文景之世日一月
而再食地一日而三震長星大水月犯
===
北辰如此之類不一而足可謂大異矣
而文景之治益以隆平宋仁宗之時土
星留參太白晝見地裂泉湧雨雹大旱
如此之類亦不為少固非小沴矣而仁
宗享國最為長久所以然者豈有他哉
亦由二聖五賢能敬承天戒故上天監
之而變災為祥耳恭惟我
皇上道高德厚治敷休明
皇天眷佑有加無已億萬年無疆之休端在是

聖心，發之而為大訓，行之而為大典，有不專在于言語文字間也？主司於此固願有聞焉。

問：自古賢聖之君，不以天無災異為可喜，惟自以德政未修為可懼。故古今論者皆以為：洪水九年而堯致治，大旱七年而湯修德，桑穀生朝而太戊中興，雉雊鼎耳而武丁道盛。漢文景之世，日一月而再食，地一日而三震，長星、大水、月犯北辰，如此之類，不一而足，可謂大異矣，而文景之治益以隆平。宋仁宗之時，土星留參，太白晝見，地裂泉湧，雨雹大旱，如此之類，亦不為少，固非小沴矣，而仁宗享國最為長久。所以然者，豈有他哉？亦由二聖五賢能敬承天戒，故上天監之而變災為祥耳。恭惟我皇上，道高德厚，治敷休明，皇天眷佑，有加無已，億萬年無疆之休，端在是
translation_en:
…within the sagely mind, issuing forth as great instructions and being put into practice as great institutions, without residing exclusively in spoken and written words? On this matter, we who preside over the examination would indeed welcome an explanation.

Question: Since antiquity, worthy and sagely rulers have not regarded Heaven’s freedom from disasters and anomalies as cause for rejoicing; rather, they have regarded their own failure to cultivate virtue and good government as cause for fear. Thus commentators past and present have all held that, despite nine years of flooding, Yao achieved good government; despite seven years of severe drought, Tang cultivated his virtue; when mulberry and paper-mulberry trees grew in the court, Taiwu restored his dynasty’s fortunes; and when a pheasant crowed on the handle of a sacrificial cauldron, Wuding’s Way flourished. During the reigns of Emperors Wen and Jing of Han, the sun was eclipsed twice in a single month, the earth shook three times in a single day, comets appeared, great floods occurred, and the moon encroached upon the Northern Pole Star. Such occurrences were too numerous to enumerate and could be called great anomalies indeed. Yet the government of Wen and Jing grew ever more prosperous and peaceful. During the reign of Emperor Renzong of Song, Saturn lingered in the Shen lunar mansion, Venus appeared in daylight, the earth split and springs gushed forth, and hailstorms and severe droughts occurred. Such events were likewise far from few and certainly were no minor disturbances. Yet Renzong’s reign was exceptionally long. Could there have been any other reason for this? It was simply that these two sages and five worthy rulers could reverently heed Heaven’s warnings. Heaven therefore watched over them and transformed disaster into good fortune.

We reverently consider that our Emperor’s Way is exalted and his virtue profound, and that his government spreads beneficence and enlightenment. August Heaven’s favor and protection increase without cease. The boundless blessings of hundreds of millions of years rest precisely upon this…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
矣然而邇年以來水旱凶荒螟蝗盜賊
之災重見疊出有未免上厪
宵旰之憂者豈非吾中外大小臣工奉行德
政有所未盡而致然歟然而
聖心高明不忍諉罪於臣下方且引咎自歸大
行寬恤之
詔欲俾天下臣民各得其所此尤吾臣子之
所以祗承
德意慚懼而不能自已者也故復欲以二聖五
賢敬天修德變災為祥之實重為
上詳陳之冀萬一有涓埃之助焉而未能也不
知諸士子其亦能精白一心具陳忠悃
俾主司得以轉聞于
上否
問士欲知天下事必先考論前代之跡深
思其治亂得失之故若身遇其時處其
事可也然前代之事多見於當時臣下
之建白後世君子之譏評是皆所當究

punctuated:
矣。然而邇年以來，水旱凶荒、螟蝗盜賊之災，重見疊出，有未免上厪宵旰之憂者，豈非吾中外大小臣工奉行德政有所未盡而致然歟？然而聖心高明，不忍諉罪於臣下，方且引咎自歸，大行寬恤之詔，欲俾天下臣民各得其所。此尤吾臣子之所以祗承德意，慚懼而不能自已者也。故復欲以二聖五賢敬天修德、變災為祥之實，重為上詳陳之，冀萬一有涓埃之助焉，而未能也。不知諸士子其亦能精白一心，具陳忠悃，俾主司得以轉聞于上否？

問：士欲知天下事，必先考論前代之跡，深思其治亂得失之故，若身遇其時、處其事可也。然前代之事，多見於當時臣下之建白、後世君子之譏評，是皆所當究
translation_en:
…indeed. Yet in recent years, disasters of flood and drought, famine, crop pests and locusts, and banditry have repeatedly arisen, inevitably adding to Your Majesty’s anxieties as you attend to affairs before dawn and until late in the day. Is this not because we officials, high and low, at court and in the provinces, have failed to carry out your benevolent policies fully? Yet Your Majesty, in your lofty wisdom, cannot bear to lay the blame upon your servants. Instead, you take responsibility yourself and widely promulgate an edict of clemency and relief, wishing all officials and common people throughout the realm to find their proper place. This makes us, your servants, all the more reverent in receiving your benevolent intentions, and unable to restrain our shame and apprehension. Thus we wish once more to set forth in detail for Your Majesty how the two sage rulers and five worthy rulers revered Heaven, cultivated virtue, and transformed calamities into auspicious signs, hoping thereby to offer even the slightest assistance. Yet we have been unable to do so. Might you candidates likewise purify and devote your hearts, fully setting forth your loyal sentiments, so that the presiding examiners may convey them to Your Majesty?

Question: A scholar who wishes to understand the affairs of the realm must first examine and discuss the events of earlier ages, pondering deeply the reasons for their order and disorder, successes and failures, as though he himself had lived in those times and dealt with those affairs. Yet the affairs of earlier ages are often recorded in the proposals submitted by officials of the time and in the critical assessments of worthy men of later generations. These are all matters that should be thoroughly…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
心者試畧舉數條與諸士論之秦廢封
建置守令後世因之間有議復封建者
何慮其非乆安之道漢變肉刑為笞法
後世亦因之間有議復肉刑者何譏其
不知本末人才學校相因也而謂長養
成就學校不與存風俗紀綱二事也而
謂禮義廉恥紀綱賴以立海內方無事
以積薪喻者曰火未及然而謂之安宰
相欲變法以居室喻者曰弊則修非大
===
壞不更造天資峭直其為三司使豈弗
堪而何木蹊田奪牛之議忠勇一心使
並佐樞府奚不可而何騰處內留邊之
奏陳便宜於西晉者欲禁民買田宅孰
病其乖簡易之制輔中興於東晉者善
因事就功孰咎其稔敦峻之亂進士之
學經史子集博學廣記將以待問河陽
判官何以曰少功而寡要牧守之職惠
綏小民古二千石兹惟其選慶曆舍人

punctuated: 心者。試畧舉數條，與諸士論之。秦廢封建，置守令，後世因之，間有議復封建者，何慮其非乆安之道？漢變肉刑為笞法，後世亦因之，間有議復肉刑者，何譏其不知本末？人才、學校相因也，而謂長養成就，學校不與存；風俗、紀綱二事也，而謂禮義廉恥，紀綱賴以立。海內方無事，以積薪喻者曰：「火未及然，而謂之安。」宰相欲變法，以居室喻者曰：「弊則修，非大壞不更造。」天資峭直，其為三司使豈弗堪？而何木蹊田奪牛之議？忠勇一心，使並佐樞府奚不可？而何騰處內留邊之奏？陳便宜於西晉者，欲禁民買田宅，孰病其乖簡易之制？輔中興於東晉者，善因事就功，孰咎其稔敦峻之亂？進士之學，經史子集，博學廣記，將以待問，河陽判官何以曰「少功而寡要」？牧守之職，惠綏小民，古二千石，兹惟其選，慶曆舍人
translation_en:
…matters to which one should give careful thought. Let us briefly raise several points for you candidates to discuss. Qin abolished feudal enfeoffment and appointed commandery governors and county magistrates; later ages followed this practice. When some proposed restoring enfeoffment, why was it feared that this was no way to secure lasting peace? Han replaced mutilating punishments with flogging, and later ages likewise followed this practice. When some proposed restoring mutilating punishments, why were they criticized for failing to distinguish root from branch?

Talent and schools are mutually dependent, yet it was said that schools had no part in nurturing talent and bringing it to fruition. Social customs and the governing order are two separate matters, yet it was said that the governing order depends upon ritual propriety, righteousness, integrity, and a sense of shame for its establishment. When all within the seas was at peace, someone used the analogy of piled firewood, saying: “The fire has not yet ignited it, and so they call it safe.” When a chief councilor wished to change the laws, someone used the analogy of a dwelling, saying: “Repair it when it becomes dilapidated; unless it is badly ruined, do not rebuild it.”

With his stern and upright disposition, how could he have been unfit to serve as Commissioner of the Finance Commission? Why, then, was there the criticism about an ox trampling a field and the ox being confiscated [?]? United in loyalty and courage, why could they not both assist in the Bureau of Military Affairs? Why, then, was there a memorial concerning Teng’s placement in the interior and retention at the frontier [?]? Of the man who presented practical proposals under Western Jin and wished to forbid the people to buy fields and houses, who criticized him for departing from a simple and straightforward system? Of the man who assisted the restoration under Eastern Jin and excelled at adapting to circumstances to achieve results, who blamed him for fostering the rebellions of Wang Dun and Su Jun?

Candidates for the metropolitan graduate degree study the classics, histories, philosophical writings, and literary collections, acquiring broad learning and extensive recall so as to be ready for questioning. Why did the Administrative Assistant of Heyang call this “yielding little result and grasping few essentials”? The duty of prefectural governors is to benefit and pacify the common people; these are the ancient officials of two thousand bushels, and selection for such posts should be fitting. The Secretariat Drafter of the Qingli era…

歸而怨嘆息莫如尚寬大佐治蜀者謂
為致敝之由俾官不虛授而職事舉莫
如久任使相貞元者謂誦老生之談凡
此皆達於國體而繫天下之治忽焉者
顧其時之所遇不同而言之獲用無幾
由今日觀之盖有不勝其可慨者矣爾

謂足食足兵安邊足用之事亦有所當

西門豹之在魏李氷之在蜀隋薛冑之

translation_en:
…why did he say, “They are not treated with sufficient regard, nor encouraged adequately”? To make everyone gladly give their allegiance, yet complain and sigh [?], nothing compares with esteeming generosity and leniency; yet one who assisted in governing Shu called this a cause of deterioration. To ensure that official appointments are not made in vain and that official duties are accomplished, nothing compares with keeping men in office for long terms; yet one who served as chief councilor during the Zhenyuan era called this the repetition of an old scholar’s commonplace talk. All these matters concern the essentials of statecraft and bear upon order or disorder throughout the realm. Yet the circumstances encountered in their times differed, and few of these proposals were adopted. Viewed from today, they surely occasion profound regret! You assembled scholars were born under a sage and enlightened ruler and have long nurtured your talents. Set forth your views fully in writing, so that we may see how you would handle the affairs of the realm in days to come.
Question: For a scholar and gentleman, there is nothing in the world that his heart ought not to cherish, and no affair that falls outside what his duty requires him to undertake. title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
在兖州唐姜師度之在易州是皆興水
利而濟用者其開鑿灌溉之法今尚有
可言者歟衞文公特小國之君耳徙居
楚丘授方任能甫及季年而革車有三
百乗之富唐張萬歲一太僕之官耳受
馬三千養于隴右而善於其職後来有

其施為牧養之術今亦有可行者歟古

===
之於渭濵其法尤為盡善不知二公之
後亦有得其遺法而奏效者歟古之鹽
筴如桑孔之言利析秋毫劉晏之權時
為輕重盖有不加賦而用足者不知三
人之後亦有可因其遺意而議行之者
歟說者又謂我
國家成憲具在各有司存今水利鹽筴二者

須别有所建明惟在厲其所以立法之

translation_en: …in Yanzhou, and Jiang Shidu of the Tang in Yizhou: all these men developed waterworks to meet practical needs. Are there aspects of their methods of excavation and irrigation that can still be discussed today? Duke Wen of Wei was merely the ruler of a small state. He moved his seat to Chuqiu, assigned responsibilities and employed capable men, and by the closing years of his reign possessed the wealth represented by three hundred war chariots. Zhang Wansui of the Tang was merely an official of the Court of the Imperial Stud. He received three thousand horses and raised them in Longyou; through his skill in performing his duties, their numbers later reached seven hundred thousand. These men all enriched their states through horse administration. Are there methods of management, pasturing, and breeding that could still be put into practice today? Among ancient military agricultural colonies, those established by Zhao Chongguo in Huangzhong and by Zhuge, Marquis of Wu, on the banks of the Wei were particularly exemplary in their methods. After these two men, were there others who inherited their methods and achieved results? In ancient salt administration, Sang and Kong discussed fiscal profit with the finest discrimination, while Liu Yan adjusted prices according to circumstances; thus there were those who secured sufficient revenue without increasing taxes. After these three men, were there also practices whose underlying principles could be followed and whose implementation might be considered? Some commentators further maintain that our dynasty’s established regulations are all in place, with responsible offices for each matter. Waterworks and salt administration, they say, will therefore naturally have their own means of dealing with affairs. title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
禁而其法行矣若夫馬政屯田之法則
非大有所建明而不可不知其說果然
歟諸士子其詳陳之毋畧
問自古盜賊之變常生於治平之世士大
夫或以為不足恤而不知其大可畏也
知其大可畏則必深思致盜之由廣詢
弭盜之術君臣上下不遑寧處其肯以
末議視之所謂致盜之由古人嘗言之
矣姑舉其一二或曰民困於饑寒而吏
===
不恤也或曰刺史無清行故吏民愁叛
或曰經畧使不得人侵欺虜縛以致怨
恨此其言豈謬歟弭盜之術古人亦嘗
言之矣或曰明賞罰之法去冗官用良
吏以撫疲民或曰盜賊者平之非難絕
之為難或曰貢舉之外別設一科以收
遺才使姦雄無徒此其謀皆善歟今天
下承平日久盜賊未息
皇上赫怒遣將分討且各

translation_en:
…the prohibitions, and these regulations will then be implemented. As for the regulations governing horse administration and military agricultural colonies, however, substantial new proposals are indispensable. Is this argument indeed correct? You candidates should set forth your views in detail, omitting nothing.
Question: Since antiquity, outbreaks of banditry have often arisen in times of peace and good order. Some scholar-officials consider them unworthy of concern, failing to recognize how greatly they are to be feared. If they recognized this, they would surely ponder deeply the causes that give rise to banditry and inquire widely into methods of suppressing it. Neither ruler nor ministers, high or low, would have leisure to rest at ease. Would they then be willing to regard it as a matter of minor importance? The ancients have already discussed these causes of banditry. Let us cite one or two examples. Some said: “The people suffer from hunger and cold, yet the officials show them no concern.” Others said: “The Regional Inspector lacks integrity in his conduct, so officials and commoners become distressed and rebel.” Others said: “An unsuitable man has been appointed Military Commissioner; his encroachments, deceptions, seizures, and fettering of people provoke resentment and hatred.” Could these statements be mistaken? The ancients also discussed methods of suppressing banditry. Some said: “Make the rules for rewards and punishments clear, remove superfluous officials, and employ good officials to soothe the exhausted people.” Others said: “It is not difficult to subdue bandits; the difficulty lies in eliminating them altogether.” Others said: “Outside the regular examination recruitment system, establish a separate examination category to recruit overlooked talent, so that unscrupulous men of ability have no followers.” Are all these proposals sound? Now the realm has enjoyed peace for many years, yet banditry has not ceased. His Majesty, in fierce anger, has dispatched generals to conduct punitive campaigns in separate areas, and in each case…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
命大臣一人節制之許以軍法從事盖將以
求天下之民安也顧師出而功有成雖
其賞屢行賊破而勢復張則我憂未已
不知所謂致之之由與弭之之術其在
今日亦若古人之所云而已邪抑尚有
可言者邪諸俊乂目擊斯患胷中必有
良策其直述以對

translation_en: …appointed one high minister to exercise overall command over each force, authorizing him to act under military law, surely with the aim of securing peace for the people throughout the realm. Yet although the armies have achieved successes in the field and rewards have repeatedly been bestowed, the rebels, once defeated, regain their strength, and our anxiety remains unabated. We wonder whether the causes that bring about such unrest and the means of suppressing it today are merely as the ancients described, or whether there is more to be said. You men of outstanding talent have witnessed this affliction firsthand and must have sound plans in mind. Set them forth candidly in your replies.

而后知至知至而后意誠
蔣承恩
同考試官給事中高批題有脉絡關鎖
此篇發揮曲盡一束尤見學力且辭理純正

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Those who wish to make their intentions sincere first extend their knowledge; extending knowledge lies in investigating things. Only after things have been investigated does knowledge reach its fullest extent; only after knowledge has reached its fullest extent do intentions become sincere.”

Jiang Cheng’en

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Supervising Secretary: The topic has an underlying thread and tightly linked connections. This essay develops them fully in all their intricacy; its concluding synthesis especially reveals the author’s scholarly attainment. Moreover, its language and reasoning are sound and orthodox, without striving for novelty or cleverness. This is writing worthy of the name.

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Examining Editor: This is the most essential work of self-cultivation in the Great Learning. Could the presiding examiners have chosen this topic casually, without a particular intention? Candidates’ essays are often merely conjectural explanations, strikingly prolix and diffuse. This essay alone fully grasps that intention. Moreover, its force and style form an integrated whole, free of superficial habits. It is included here to admonish those who chase current fashions and delight in novelty.

Comment by Associate Examiner Jing, Compiler: Clear, upright, and dignified, it is especially brilliant in bringing out the turning points and crucial connections. It is sufficient to demonstrate standards and methods to all under Heaven.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Compiler: In essays expounding the Great Learning, candidates in the examination hall use excessive words and repeat their ideas, becoming tiresomely entangled. This essay alone presents its exposition clearly and in good order, reducing extensive material to concise expression. Its author is a scholar skilled in explaining principle. It is included here to instruct scholars throughout the realm; writing that merely pieces together ornate phrases…

大學論自脩明善之有序而必覆言其意焉蓋

translation_en:
…such writing should thereby undergo a transformation.
Examiner Mao, Academician, comments: The language and reasoning are sound and substantial, and the vital force is also abundant. Readers should appreciate this for themselves.
Examiner Liang, Grand Secretary, comments: The author has integrated the meanings of the Commentary in Chapters and Sentences (Zhangju) and the Questions and Answers (Huowen) into his composition. This is why it merits inclusion.
The Great Learning discusses the ordered sequence of cultivating oneself and understanding goodness, yet also insists on restating its meaning. Making the intentions sincere is the first step in cultivating oneself, while investigating things and extending knowledge are essential to understanding goodness. This sequence certainly must not be confused. Having expounded the sequence, the Great Learning then restates its meaning. How earnest is its intention to instruct people! The meaning of the canonical text of the Great Learning is as though it said: The way to govern the state and bring peace to the world has its foundation in cultivating oneself; and the way to cultivate oneself begins with making the intentions sincere. If the intentions lack sincerity, there is no foundation for rectifying the mind and cultivating oneself. Yet people know that their intentions ought to be sincere without knowing that their knowledge ought to be extended to the utmost. If the work of extending knowledge remains incomplete in any respect, truth and falsehood become intermingled in the hidden and subtle recesses of the mind. Even if one wishes to force oneself to make the intentions sincere, there will be intentions that cannot be made sincere. Thus, anyone wishing to make the intentions sincere must first find the means to extend their knowledge to the utmost. Knowledge within oneself must certainly be fully developed, but principle within things must above all be investigated exhaustively. If the work of investigating things falls short in any respect, then wherever principle has not been fully fathomed, knowledge must be obscured. Even if one wishes to force oneself to extend knowledge to the utmost, there will be knowledge that cannot be so extended. title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
於有以格乎事物之理焉夫自脩明善之序其
不可紊也如此為大人之學者誠能隨事觀理
極深研幾使理之在物者各有以詣其極而無
餘則知之在我者亦隨所詣而無不盡矣知其
有不至者乎理既克明知無不盡則心之所發
能一於理凡欲為善以去惡必能自慊而無自
欺矣意豈有不由此而誠者乎夫物格而知以
至則致知之在格物也明矣知至而意以誠則
誠意之在致知也審矣自非大學推言於先覆
===
言於後人亦孰從而知之也哉大抵經文一章
以明德新民止至善三者為之綱以格致誠正
脩齊治平八者為之目盖脩身以上明明德之
事也齊家以下新民之事也物格知至則知所
止矣意誠以下則皆得所止之序也先儒謂大
學一書總而言之不出乎八事而八事之要總
而言之又不出乎此三言學者合經文十傳而
並觀之則可見矣嗚呼此其所以為古者大學
教人之法也乎

punctuated:
於有以格乎事物之理焉。夫自脩明善之序，其不可紊也如此。為大人之學者，誠能隨事觀理，極深研幾，使理之在物者各有以詣其極而無餘，則知之在我者亦隨所詣而無不盡矣。知其有不至者乎？理既克明，知無不盡，則心之所發能一於理，凡欲為善以去惡，必能自慊而無自欺矣。意豈有不由此而誠者乎？夫物格而知以至，則致知之在格物也明矣；知至而意以誠，則誠意之在致知也審矣。自非《大學》推言於先，覆言於後，人亦孰從而知之也哉？
大抵經文一章，以明德、新民、止至善三者為之綱，以格、致、誠、正、脩、齊、治、平八者為之目。盖脩身以上，明明德之事也；齊家以下，新民之事也。物格知至，則知所止矣；意誠以下，則皆得所止之序也。先儒謂《大學》一書，總而言之，不出乎八事；而八事之要，總而言之，又不出乎此三言。學者合經文十傳而並觀之，則可見矣。嗚呼！此其所以為古者大學教人之法也乎！
translation_en:
…in finding the means to investigate the principles of affairs and things. Such is the inviolable sequence of cultivating oneself and understanding goodness. Those pursuing the learning of the great person, if they can truly examine principles in each affair, plumb their depths, and scrutinize their subtlest beginnings, will bring their investigation of the principles inherent in things to its utmost extent, leaving nothing unexplored. Their own knowledge will likewise become complete as their investigation advances. Could any of their knowledge then fail to reach its full extent? Once principles have been clearly understood and knowledge is complete, whatever issues from the mind can accord wholly with principle. Whenever they wish to do good and remove evil, they will assuredly find satisfaction within themselves, without self-deception. How could their intentions fail thereby to become sincere? When things have been investigated and knowledge consequently reaches its full extent, it is clear that extending knowledge lies in investigating things. When knowledge reaches its full extent and intentions consequently become sincere, it is certain that making intentions sincere lies in extending knowledge. Had the Great Learning not first set this forth and then restated it afterward, how could people have come to understand it?
Broadly speaking, the single chapter of the canonical text takes three things as its guiding principles: manifesting luminous virtue, renewing the people, and resting in the highest good. Its eight particulars are investigating things, extending knowledge, making intentions sincere, rectifying the mind, cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to all under Heaven. Cultivating oneself and the preceding steps concern manifesting luminous virtue; regulating the family and the subsequent steps concern renewing the people. Once things have been investigated and knowledge has reached its full extent, one knows where to rest. Making intentions sincere and the subsequent steps constitute the sequence through which one attains that resting place. Earlier Confucian scholars said that the Great Learning, taken as a whole, does not go beyond these eight matters; and that the essentials of these eight matters, taken as a whole, do not go beyond these three phrases. Students can see this by considering the canonical text together with its ten chapters of commentary. Ah! Is this not what constitutes the method by which the Great Learning of antiquity taught people?

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
夫子之文章可得而聞也夫子之言性與
天道不可得而聞也
蔡昂
同考試官署員外郎陳批子貢善觀聖
人晩年進德始發此嘆非因文章中悟性與
天道也此作能得其旨而描寫殆盡盖嘗究
心於道者矣豈徒有得文章而已哉
同考試官編修張批題本明白作者多
務浮冗不能檃括為文往往沉晦此直以溫
===
雅平易之辭發之而理道即躍然目前要亦
得其雋永者
同考試官編修趙批論語義士子率能
組織成篇然冗長無叙此作嚴正簡古必究
心于內者錄之
同考試官編修黃批士子於不可得聞
處多失旨此作融會傳註寫出子貢之意故
錄之
考試官學士毛批講語親切取之

天道不可得而聞也
蔡昂

〔雅平易之辭發之而理道即躍然目前要亦〕
===
〔得其雋永者〕
同考試官編修趙　批　〔論語義士子率能組織成篇然冗長無叙此作嚴正簡古必究〕
〔心于内者錄之〕
同考試官編修黃　批　〔士子於不可得聞處多失旨此作融會傳註寫出子貢之意故〕
〔錄之〕
考試官學士毛　批　〔講語親切取之〕
punctuated:
夫子之文章，可得而聞也；夫子之言性與天道，不可得而聞也。
蔡昂。
同考試官署員外郎陳批：子貢善觀聖人，晩年進德，始發此嘆，非因文章中悟性與天道也。此作能得其旨，而描寫殆盡，盖嘗究心於道者矣，豈徒有得文章而已哉！
同考試官編修張批：題本明白，作者多務浮冗，不能檃括為文，往往沉晦。此直以溫雅平易之辭發之，而理道即躍然目前，要亦得其雋永者。
同考試官編修趙批：《論語》義，士子率能組織成篇，然冗長無叙。此作嚴正簡古，必究心于內者，錄之。
同考試官編修黃批：士子於不可得聞處多失旨，此作融會傳註，寫出子貢之意，故錄之。
考試官學士毛批：講語親切，取之。
translation_en:
“The Master’s cultural accomplishments can be heard about; his words on human nature and the Way of Heaven cannot be heard.”
Cai Ang.
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Acting Vice Director: Zigong was adept at observing the sage. Only in his later years, after advancing in virtue, did he voice this sigh; it was not that he had apprehended human nature and the Way of Heaven through the Master’s cultural accomplishments. This composition grasps that purport and sets it forth almost exhaustively. Its author must have devoted thought to the Way. Could his understanding be confined to cultural accomplishments alone?
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Compiler: The topic is clear in itself, but writers often pursue superficial elaboration and cannot draw its meaning together into an essay, frequently becoming obscure. This composition expresses it directly in language that is refined, gentle, plain, and accessible, so that the underlying principles spring vividly before one’s eyes. In essence, it captures the topic’s enduring savor.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Compiler: On the meaning of the Analects, candidates can generally put together an essay, but their compositions are lengthy and disordered. This composition is disciplined and correct, concise and classically restrained. Its author must have given earnest thought to its inner meaning. Select it.
Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Compiler: Candidates often miss the purport of the phrase “cannot be heard.” This composition integrates the commentaries and annotations and conveys Zigong’s meaning; it is therefore selected.
Comment by Examiner Mao, Academician: The exposition is apt and direct. Accept it.

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
考試官大學士梁批能發明聖人教不躐
等之意可取
聖人常示人以德之顯者而不輕語人以理之
微者盖文章顯而性與天道微也聖人教不躐
等此學者所以聞之有難易歟吾想夫子貢之
意若曰夫子之德合內外而一致夫子之教隨
高下而異施是故威儀之著可畏可象文辭之
發至易至簡燦然有文也蔚然有章也斯其所
性施於四體和順發于英華煥乎日星之呈露
===
而未嘗隱也故雖互鄉童子猶得以望見於門
墻而況從游之士以衛之封人猶得以觀感其
氣象而況親炙之徒是夫子之文章在學者固
可得而聞也非以其顯而易見乎至若人生而
靜性其固有惟天為大道體無窮萬物一原也
萬殊一本也是惟聖愚同得之理造化流行之
妙寂乎聲臭之不聞而未易窺也故雅言者
詩書執禮而是理也非真積力久者不輕告四
教者文行忠信而是道也非深造自得者不强

詩書執禮而是理也非真積力久者不輕告四
教者文行忠信而是道也非深造自得者不强
punctuated:
考試官大學士梁批：能發明聖人教不躐等之意，可取。

聖人常示人以德之顯者，而不輕語人以理之微者，盖文章顯而性與天道微也。聖人教不躐等，此學者所以聞之有難易歟？吾想夫子貢之意若曰：夫子之德合內外而一致，夫子之教隨高下而異施。是故威儀之著，可畏可象；文辭之發，至易至簡。燦然有文也，蔚然有章也。斯其所性施於四體，和順發于英華，煥乎日星之呈露，而未嘗隱也。故雖互鄉童子，猶得以望見於門墻，而況從游之士；以衛之封人，猶得以觀感其氣象，而況親炙之徒。是夫子之文章，在學者固可得而聞也，非以其顯而易見乎？至若人生而靜，性其固有；惟天為大，道體無窮。萬物一原也，萬殊一本也。是惟聖愚同得之理，造化流行之妙，寂乎聲臭之不聞，而未易窺也。故雅言者，詩、書、執禮，而是理也，非真積力久者不輕告；四教者，文、行、忠、信，而是道也，非深造自得者不强
translation_en:
Examiner Grand Secretary Liang comments: This succeeds in elucidating the idea that the sage’s teaching does not skip stages. It merits selection.

The sage regularly shows people the manifest aspects of his virtue, but does not lightly speak to them of the subtleties of principle. For his cultural accomplishments are manifest, whereas human nature and the Way of Heaven are subtle. The sage’s teaching does not skip stages: is this why some things are easy for learners to hear about, while others are difficult? I imagine Zigong’s meaning to have been as follows: The Master’s virtue unites the inner and outer in a single whole; his teaching varies according to the higher or lower attainments of those he teaches. Thus, his bearing, visibly displayed, inspires awe and invites emulation; his words, when expressed, are utterly accessible and simple. How brilliantly patterned, how richly accomplished! What belongs to his nature is expressed through his four limbs; harmony and accord blossom into splendid expression. These shine forth like the sun and stars, never concealed. Thus even a boy from Huxiang could glimpse him at his gates and walls—how much more those who followed him in study! Even the frontier guard of Wei could observe his presence and be moved by it—how much more the disciples who received his instruction directly! The Master’s cultural accomplishments were indeed something learners could hear about. Was this not because they were manifest and easy to perceive?

As for human beings being still at birth, their nature is inherently theirs; Heaven alone is great, and the substance of the Way is inexhaustible. The myriad things have a single source; their countless differences have a single root. This is the principle equally received by sage and fool, the wondrous workings of creation as it flows onward. Silent, without perceptible sound or smell, it cannot readily be glimpsed. Thus the subjects of his customary discourse were the Book of Odes, the Book of Documents, and the observance of ritual; but this principle he did not lightly disclose to anyone who had not sincerely accumulated learning and exerted effort over a long time. His four subjects of instruction were cultural learning, conduct, loyalty, and trustworthiness; but this Way, for those who had not studied deeply and attained understanding for themselves, he would not press…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
聒是夫子之言性與天道在學者則不可得而
聞也非以其微而難知乎子貢之為是言豈非
自以夫子之至論昔者未聞至是始得聞之而
嘆其美也哉雖然性與天道一也文章其發於
外者耳顧夫子之文章惟見於吾身不若堯之
文章見於治天下此其有不同者易曰乾道變
化各正性命又曰一陰一陽之謂道繼之者善
成之者性子貢之所聞殆此乎吁夫子之窮其
文章雖不得同乎堯其性與天道之說存乎易
===
者萬世如見豈非後學之幸哉
於季桓子見行可之仕也
張璁
同考試官署員外郎黃 批 孟子嘗說夫
子去魯之事衆人不識此作於見行可處發
明夫子仕魯之意婉曲詳盡亦有衆人所不
識者讀之起敬
同考試官給事中王 批 題乃全聖之時
底意思作者類多拘滯幾至誣吾夫子者亦

於季桓子見行可之仕也
張　鏊
同考試官署員外郎黃　批　孟子嘗說夫
子去魯之事衆人不識此作於見行可處發
明夫子仕魯之意婉曲詳盡亦有衆人所不
識者讀之起敬
同考試官給事中王　批　題與會聖之時
底意思作者類多拘滯幾至誣吾夫子者亦
punctuated:
聒。是夫子之言性與天道，在學者則不可得而聞也，非以其微而難知乎？子貢之為是言，豈非自以夫子之至論，昔者未聞，至是始得聞之，而嘆其美也哉？雖然，性與天道一也，文章其發於外者耳。顧夫子之文章惟見於吾身，不若堯之文章見於治天下，此其有不同者。《易》曰：「乾道變化，各正性命。」又曰：「一陰一陽之謂道，繼之者善，成之者性。」子貢之所聞殆此乎？吁！夫子之窮其文章，雖不得同乎堯，其性與天道之說存乎《易》者，萬世如見，豈非後學之幸哉？
於季桓子見行可之仕也。
張璁
同考試官署員外郎黃批：孟子嘗說夫子去魯之事，衆人不識。此作於見行可處，發明夫子仕魯之意，婉曲詳盡，亦有衆人所不識者，讀之起敬。
同考試官給事中王批：題乃全聖之時底意思，作者類多拘滯，幾至誣吾夫子者亦
translation_en:
… importune them. Thus, learners could not obtain a hearing of the Master's words on human nature and the Way of Heaven. Was this not because these were subtle and difficult to understand? When Zigong spoke these words, was it not because he himself had never previously heard the Master's highest teachings, had only now first heard them, and was expressing admiration for their excellence? Nevertheless, human nature and the Way of Heaven are one; cultivated accomplishments are simply their outward expression. Yet the Master's cultivated accomplishments were manifested only in his own person, unlike Yao's, which were manifested in governing all under Heaven. Here lay their difference. The Book of Changes says: “The Way of Qian changes and transforms, and each being attains its proper nature and allotted destiny.” It also says: “One yin and one yang are called the Way. What continues it is goodness; what completes it is human nature.” Was what Zigong heard perhaps this? Ah! Although the Master could not equal Yao in fully realizing his cultivated accomplishments, his teachings on human nature and the Way of Heaven survive in the Book of Changes, as though visible before us for ten thousand generations. Is this not fortunate for later learners?
“With Ji Huanzi, he took office because he saw that his Way could be put into practice.”
Zhang Cong
Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Acting Vice Director: Mencius once explained the circumstances of the Master's departure from Lu, but most people do not understand them. This essay elucidates the Master's intention in taking office in Lu through the phrase “saw that his Way could be put into practice.” Its treatment is nuanced and exhaustive, and contains insights that most people likewise fail to recognize. Reading it inspires respect.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Supervising Secretary: The topic conveys the full meaning of the sage's timeliness [?]. Most writers are constrained and inflexible in their interpretations; there are even those who come close to slandering our Master …

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
有之此作意正語圓且發揮見字尤為親切
意予可謂善言聖人者矣
同考試官編修許批孔子仕本為道作
者類冗泛陳言使孔子之心不白殊可厭也
此獨辭不費而理到出處之義行道之權有
宛然在目者宜錄以破羣疑
同考試官編修翟批孔子本仕魯而曰
於季桓子正見道之可行處作者不察遂以
為真仕季桓非矣是篇語有斟酌文更純雅
===
一洗俗見之陋宜錄以示學者
同考試官右中允李批此作能道孔子
心事且命辭老健是可以式矣

暢而有事實與冗泛者大異矣

考試官大學士梁批：辭能達意，可取。

聖人之仕於魯，以其道有可行之兆也。蓋聖人之仕止，一道之所在也。道既有可行之兆，聖人又安得而不仕乎？昔孟子因萬章交際之問而
translation_en:
…there are indeed such cases. This essay is sound in its purport and well rounded in its expression; its elucidation of the word “perceived” is especially apt. In my judgment [?], its author may be called someone who speaks well of the Sage.

Associate Examiner Xu, Compiler, comments: Confucius took office fundamentally for the sake of the Way. Writers generally offer verbose, vague platitudes that leave Confucius’s intentions obscure—a most disagreeable failing. This essay alone reaches the principle without wasting words. The rightness of taking office or withdrawing, and the discretionary judgment involved in putting the Way into practice, stand vividly before our eyes. It should be included to dispel the many doubts.

Associate Examiner Zhai, Compiler, comments: Confucius actually served the state of Lu. The wording “with Ji Huanzi” points precisely to the circumstances in which the Way could be put into practice. Writers fail to examine this and consequently suppose that he actually served Ji Huanzi; this is mistaken. This essay’s wording is judicious, and its prose particularly refined and elegant. It sweeps away the crudity of commonplace interpretations and should be included for students to see.

Associate Examiner Li, Right Mentor, comments: This essay conveys what was in Confucius’s heart, and its phrasing is mature and vigorous. It can serve as a model.

Examiner Mao, Academician, comments: In discussing Confucius’s service in Lu, the language is lucid and fluent, and the account is grounded in historical facts. It differs greatly from verbose and vague compositions.

孔子之道義方隆而桓子之向慕亦切故始焉
宰中都歷司寇雖由定公能用之亦由桓子能

…answered him with the cases of Confucius’s service in Lu and Wei. His meaning was that when Duke Ding of Lu employed Confucius, it was precisely the time when Ji Huanzi controlled Lu’s government. At that time, Confucius’s moral authority was growing, and Huanzi’s admiration for him was also earnest. Thus, at first, Confucius served as magistrate of Zhongdu and then as Minister of Justice. This was owing both to Duke Ding’s ability to employ him and to Huanzi’s willingness to accommodate him: there was some hope that our Way could be put into practice. They supposed that Confucius’s Way could henceforth be put into practice, not realizing that when he first entered office, Confucius had already foreseen signs of precisely this outcome. Could he have merely experimented and acted without due consideration? People saw that when he acted as chief minister, Zheng Mao [?] was executed, and that when he participated in government, Lu became well governed. …in excellence, no essay on the meaning of the classic equals this one. Such an achievement is beyond those who merely parade empty phrases without inward understanding.

Associate Examiner Li, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: In writing on the learning of principle, choosing words is difficult. If even one expression is used carelessly, the result will be either cumbersome or obscure. To be classical yet clear, profound yet free of eccentricity, as this essay is, may indeed be called difficult.

Examiner Mao, a Hanlin Academician, comments: Other essays mostly treat the word “established” lightly. This one alone does otherwise; that is why I selected it.

Examiner Liang, a Grand Secretary, comments: It is difficult to expound fully the meaning of the Book of Changes. This essay has, perhaps, succeeded.

The Commentary on the Words of the Text discusses how the noble man advances his inward and outward learning together, thereby bringing his virtue to fullness. For virtue must depend upon learning for its completion. When the noble man’s learning reaches the point at which reverence and rightness are established together, how could his virtue fail to flourish accordingly? In the Commentary on the Words of the Text, the sage uses the noble man’s learning to elaborate the meaning of the Commentary on the Images for the second, yin line of Kun. He holds that the human heart-mind is upright in its original substance and square in its judgments and ordering of affairs. Yet many, failing to understand this, lose it. The noble man holds that nothing equals reverence for nurturing the heart-mind. Thus he constantly maintains awe and apprehension, never relaxing for a moment; he remains solemn, respectful, and watchful, never becoming lax when there is nothing to do. Such is his commitment to reverence. Consequently, within the small compass of his heart-mind, he is expansively impartial, without any obscuration, wholly and supremely upright, without the slightest bias. This penetrates above and below, like a mirror empty of anything of its own. How could his inward self fail to be straight [two illegible characters: □□]? …

移左之右之如矩斯絜外其有不方邪然君子

translation_en:
…For regulating affairs, nothing surpasses righteousness. Thus, by examining principles in things, one distinguishes what is appropriate in the multitude of affairs; by plumbing the depths and investigating the incipient signs of change, one fully realizes the mind’s capacity to judge. Such is the noble man’s adherence to righteousness. Consequently, in responding to affairs, his decisions are orderly and unconfused, and his determination of right and wrong is settled and unwavering. Turning left or right, he measures as with a carpenter’s square: how could his outward conduct fail to be square? Yet could the attainments of the noble man’s learning stop at this alone?

His efforts in reverent attentiveness and righteousness cultivate each other without cease, through both activity and stillness. Over time, practice becomes second nature, bringing the subtle attainment of dwelling securely in the Way and drawing deeply upon its resources. All the virtue gathered in himself then naturally renews itself day after day, reaching its utmost greatness without standing alone. In learning directed both inward and outward, he neither forgets his efforts nor forces their growth; the two continually sustain each other. At the highest attainment, the Way becomes inseparable from his person, and he possesses the goodness that perfects himself and extends to other things. All the virtue stored within then naturally becomes full and radiant, reaching complete wholeness without partiality.

Ah! Being straight and square means proceeding from substance to function: this is the meaning of closing and opening. Not standing alone means advancing from greatness toward sagehood: this is union without bounds. Surely this is how the noble man embodies the Way of Kun, the Receptive, without interruption!

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
聖人治化之妙順乎理而獲乎天也夫聖人治
天下順易理以為之耳其獲乎天而吉无不利
也有以哉此黃帝堯舜之事孔子於易傳言之
所以明其制器尚象也蓋謂聖人之治雖一本
乎道所以為治則各因乎時彼時之趨者變也
其趨也蓋莫知所適之塗惟聖人為能推而行
之凡所以通其變者修之皆道之自然風動之
餘民皆甘說道而不以為勞夙而興夜而寐亹
亹從事其孰能已之變之成者化也其成也蓋
===
必有發動之機惟聖人為能鼓之舞之凡所以
導其化者泯乎无迹之可求涵泳之久民皆順
帝則而不以為力出而作入而息皞皞自得其
孰不宜之然此豈強為之哉蓋天地陰陽之理
有消息盈虛之道所謂易也故時過而其數也
終則物不能以不窮物窮而其運也息則勢不
容於不變惟變也則周流不滯而可通惟通也
則運用有常而可久是知易之理即天之道而
聖人則有以順之矣其不得天之助乎故文章

punctuated: 聖人治化之妙，順乎理而獲乎天也。夫聖人治天下，順易理以為之耳。其獲乎天而吉无不利也，有以哉！此黃帝堯舜之事，孔子於易傳言之，所以明其制器尚象也。蓋謂聖人之治，雖一本乎道，所以為治則各因乎時。彼時之趨者，變也。其趨也，蓋莫知所適之塗，惟聖人為能推而行之。凡所以通其變者，修之皆道之自然。風動之餘，民皆甘說道而不以為勞，夙而興，夜而寐，亹亹從事，其孰能已之？變之成者，化也。其成也，蓋必有發動之機，惟聖人為能鼓之舞之。凡所以導其化者，泯乎无迹之可求。涵泳之久，民皆順帝則而不以為力，出而作，入而息，皞皞自得，其孰不宜之？然此豈強為之哉？蓋天地陰陽之理，有消息盈虛之道，所謂易也。故時過而其數也終，則物不能以不窮；物窮而其運也息，則勢不容於不變。惟變也，則周流不滯而可通；惟通也，則運用有常而可久。是知易之理即天之道，而聖人則有以順之矣。其不得天之助乎？故文章
translation_en:
The subtle excellence of the sages’ governance and transforming influence lies in following principle and gaining Heaven’s favor. In governing the world, the sages merely act in accordance with the principles of the Changes. There is indeed a reason why they gain Heaven’s favor, enjoy good fortune, and find nothing unfavorable! These were the deeds of Huangdi, Yao, and Shun. Confucius spoke of them in the Commentary on the Changes to explain how they esteemed its images when fashioning implements.

The meaning is that, although the sages’ government is wholly rooted in the Way, their means of governing always accord with the times. The movement of the times is change. As it proceeds, no one knows the path it will take; only the sages can advance it and put it into effect. Whatever they cultivate to carry these changes through accords with the natural course of the Way. Once their influence has moved the people like the wind, all gladly delight in the Way [?] and do not regard their efforts as toil. Rising early and sleeping late, they apply themselves diligently to their tasks: who could bring them to a halt?

The completion of change is transformation. Its completion must have an initiating impulse; only the sages can rouse and animate it. In all their means of guiding this transformation, no trace of deliberate action can be found. After long immersion in their influence, the people all follow the Supreme Lord’s standards without feeling that they exert themselves. They go out to work and return to rest, contentedly at ease: who would not find this fitting? Yet how could this be achieved by force?

The principles of Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, comprise the course of waning and waxing, fullness and emptiness: this is what is called the Changes. Thus, when a time has passed and its allotted span has ended, things inevitably reach exhaustion. When things are exhausted and their movement ceases, circumstances necessarily demand change. Only through change can they circulate without obstruction and achieve free passage; only through free passage can their operation possess constancy and endure. From this we know that the principles of the Changes are the Way of Heaven, and that the sages possess the means to follow them. How could they fail to receive Heaven’s assistance? translation_en:
…institutions attain complete excellence and perfection; moral principles are unified and customs are shared. What good fortune could compare with this? The Way of the Changes moves with the times, and the sages have the means to put it into practice. Would they not receive Heaven’s blessing? Thus the common people feel neither hatred nor weariness, the many affairs of government are harmoniously ordered, and moral instruction reaches everywhere. What, then, would not be favorable? Heaven responds above through accord, and the people are governed below through accord. What action, indeed, need Huangdi, Yao, and Shun take in their midst?

Yet why does Confucius here draw his images from Qian and Kun? Surely the union of yin and yang in potency, bringing about transformation without deliberate action, is both the profound meaning of the Changes and the Way of high antiquity. When he arranged the Documents, he began with Tang and Yu. Was this not because the mutual accord of their rulers and ministers constituted an unparalleled flourishing of imperial and royal government? From the Han and Jin onward, change remained as inexhaustible as in antiquity; yet none brought about good government in accordance with the times as those ancient emperors and kings had done. The abuses that developed all arose from erring through excess or insufficiency. This is Confucius’s profound meaning, which those charged with adapting to change ought to understand.

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
乎君心而治忽觀乎民情彼水火金木土穀之
六府正德利用厚生之三事皆國之所以養民
者是之謂九功夫六府未修三事未和不可以
言叙今則天者成而無或缺人者備而無所乖
曰府曰事各順其理而不汨陳以亂其常九功
何如其叙邪夫九功不叙羣生不遂安得而有
歌今則府事治而安養賴膏澤沐而憂戚忘庶
民百姓各得其所而皆永言以詠其情九叙豈
無其歌邪夫如是則養民之功成矣然人之勤
怠者或不齊上之人安可無激勵之道哉故必
設為從容化導之方其勤於是者則戒諭而休
美之使志有所慕而益勤其怠於是者則督責
而懲戒之使心有所畏而知警然事之勉强者
不能久上之人又可無勸相之道哉故復即其
前日歌詠之言協之律呂而用之鄉人于以鼓
舞其志意俾修和之功久存而不墜播之聲音
而用之邦國于以感發其心思俾府事之績日
新而不壞夫如是則保治之道得矣吁養民於

乎君心而治忽觀乎民尚彼水火金木土穀之
六府正德利用厚生之三事皆國之所以養民
者是之謂九功夫六府未修三事未和不可以
言叙今則天者成而無或缺人者備而無所乖
曰府曰事各順其理而不汨陳以亂其常九功
何如其叙邪夫九功不叙羣生不遂安得而有
歌今則府事治而安養賴膏澤沐而憂戚忘庶
民百姓各得其所而皆永言以詠其情九叙豈
無其歌邪夫如是則養民之功成矣然人之勤

設爲從容化導之方其勤於是者則戒喻而俾
美之使志有所慕而益勤其怠於是者則督責
而懲戒之使心有所畏而知警然事之勉强者
不能久上之人又可無勸相之道哉故復即其
前日歌詠之言協之律呂而用之鄉人用之邦

而用之邦國于以感發其心思俾府事之績日

punctuated: 乎君心，而治忽觀乎民情。彼水火金木土穀之六府，正德利用厚生之三事，皆國之所以養民者，是之謂九功。夫六府未修，三事未和，不可以言叙。今則天者成而無或缺，人者備而無所乖，曰府曰事，各順其理，而不汨陳以亂其常，九功何如其叙邪？夫九功不叙，羣生不遂，安得而有歌？今則府事治而安養賴，膏澤沐而憂戚忘，庶民百姓各得其所，而皆永言以詠其情，九叙豈無其歌邪？夫如是，則養民之功成矣。然人之勤怠者或不齊，上之人安可無激勵之道哉？故必設為從容化導之方，其勤於是者，則戒諭而休美之，使志有所慕而益勤；其怠於是者，則督責而懲戒之，使心有所畏而知警。然事之勉强者不能久，上之人又可無勸相之道哉？故復即其前日歌詠之言，協之律呂而用之鄉人，于以鼓舞其志意，俾修和之功久存而不墜；播之聲音而用之邦國，于以感發其心思，俾府事之績日新而不壞。夫如是，則保治之道得矣。吁！養民於

…in the ruler’s heart, while good government or neglect is discerned in the condition of the people. The six resources—water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain—and the three undertakings—rectifying virtue, facilitating use, and enriching livelihood—are all means by which the state nourishes the people. These are called the nine achievements. When the six resources have not been properly managed and the three undertakings have not been harmonized, one cannot speak of their being in order. Now, however, what pertains to Heaven is accomplished without deficiency, and what pertains to human effort is fully provided without discord. Resources and undertakings alike follow their proper principles, without disrupting their arrangement and throwing their constant order into confusion. How well ordered, then, are the nine achievements! If the nine achievements were not in order and living beings could not flourish, how could there be songs? Now the resources and undertakings are well governed, providing a basis for peaceful sustenance; the people are bathed in beneficence and forget their sorrows. The common people all find their proper places and prolong their words in song to express their feelings. With the nine achievements thus ordered, how could there be no songs celebrating them? In this way, the work of nourishing the people is accomplished.

Yet people may differ in diligence and negligence. How could those above them dispense with means of encouragement? They must therefore devise ways to transform and guide them gently. Those who are diligent in these matters should be admonished, instructed, and praised, so that their aspirations have something to look toward and they become still more diligent. Those who are negligent should be supervised, reproved, and disciplined, so that they have something to fear and learn vigilance. Yet work performed under compulsion cannot endure. How, then, could those above them dispense with means of encouragement and assistance? Accordingly, they should take the words previously sung, harmonize them with the pitch standards, and employ them among the people of the local communities. In this way they inspire their resolve, so that the achievements of proper management and harmonization endure without lapsing. They should set these words to music and employ them throughout the states, thereby stirring people’s hearts and thoughts, so that accomplishments concerning the resources and undertakings are renewed daily and do not decay. In this way, the means of preserving good government are attained. Ah! To nourish the people in…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
平日而保治於無窮古人之謀國其慮之遠如
是乎抑觀虞廷之臣相與陳謨於君各盡其道
盖警戒之辭甚切而謀猷之道愈詳故能成雍
熙泰和之化夷考其政不過本之於德成之於
樂耳若周禮以大司樂美風俗亦其遺意也後
世此意不復而訓辭尚存雖不能播之鄉國而
猶講之學校舉而行之亦何患民之不化哉
以覲文王之耿光以揚武王之大烈
曹鈇
===
同考試官署員外郎陳批周公詰兵之
訓盖先事而憂國者故其立言必本諸繼先
王德業是豈導成王於得已而用之哉作者
多昧此意纔講到覲揚處便脫畧發明詳盡
僅見此篇宜錄以示式
同考試官編修張批文武許大勲德周
公纔兩言便盡且覲揚之責從詰兵中來固
有難於發揮者是作體貼經傳而命意修辭
亦自雅重視他浮艷之說祇增厭耳

平日而保治於無窮古人之謀國其慮之遠如
是乎抑觀虞廷之臣相與陳說於君者盡其道
蓋警戒之辭甚切而謀猷之道愈詳故能成雍
熙泰和之化夷考其政不過本之於德成之於
樂耳若周禮以大司樂美風俗亦其遺意也後
世此意不復而訓辭尚存雖不能播之鄉國而
猶講之學校舉而行之亦何患民之不化哉
以觀文王之耿光以揚武王之大烈
曹鉉
===
同考試官署員外郎陳　批　〔周公詰兵之〕
訓蓋先事而憂國者故其立言必要諸勝先
王德業是宣導成王於得已而用之義作者
多昧此意纔講到覲揚處便䟽畧發明詳盡
僅見此篇宜錄以示式
同考試官編修張　批　〔文武許大無德周〕
公纔兩言便盡且覲揚之責從詰兵中來回
有難於發揮者是作體貼經傳而命意修辭
亦自雅重視他浮豔之說獨增嚴耳
punctuated:
平日而保治於無窮，古人之謀國，其慮之遠如是乎？抑觀虞廷之臣，相與陳謨於君，各盡其道。盖警戒之辭甚切，而謀猷之道愈詳，故能成雍熙泰和之化。夷考其政，不過本之於德，成之於樂耳。若《周禮》以大司樂美風俗，亦其遺意也。後世此意不復，而訓辭尚存，雖不能播之鄉國，而猶講之學校，舉而行之，亦何患民之不化哉？
「以覲文王之耿光，以揚武王之大烈。」
曹鈇
同考試官署員外郎陳批：「周公詰兵之訓，盖先事而憂國者，故其立言必本諸繼先王德業，是豈導成王於得已而用之哉？作者多昧此意，纔講到覲揚處便脫畧，發明詳盡，僅見此篇，宜錄以示式。」
同考試官編修張批：「文武許大勲德，周公纔兩言便盡，且覲揚之責從詰兵中來，固有難於發揮者。是作體貼經傳，而命意修辭亦自雅重，視他浮艷之說，祇增厭耳。」
translation_en:
…in ordinary times and preserve good government forever: was the foresight of the ancients in planning for their state truly so far-reaching? Consider, moreover, the ministers at the court of Yu, who together presented counsels to their ruler, each fully expounding his way. Their words of admonition were most earnest, and their counsels increasingly detailed; thus they could achieve a transformation characterized by harmony, prosperity, and great peace. Examining their government dispassionately, we find that they merely grounded it in virtue and perfected it through music. The use of the Musician-in-chief to improve customs in the Rites of Zhou likewise preserves this intent. In later ages this intent was no longer realized, yet the words of instruction survived. Even if they could not be disseminated throughout the districts and states, they were still expounded in the schools. If these teachings were put into practice, why worry that the people would not be transformed?
“To make manifest King Wen’s brilliant glory and to exalt King Wu’s great achievements.”
Cao Fu
Associate Examiner Chen, Acting Vice Director, comments: “The Duke of Zhou’s instruction to put the troops in order arose from concern for the state before events occurred. Hence his words necessarily took as their foundation the continuation of the former kings’ virtue and achievements. Could he have been guiding King Cheng to employ troops when he could have refrained? Most writers fail to grasp this intent; as soon as they reach the words ‘make manifest’ and ‘exalt,’ their treatment becomes cursory. Only in this essay have I seen a thorough elucidation. It should be recorded to serve as a model.”
Associate Examiner Zhang, Hanlin Compiler, comments: “So great were the achievements and virtues of Kings Wen and Wu, yet the Duke of Zhou encompassed them in just two phrases. Moreover, the duty to ‘make manifest’ and ‘exalt’ arises from putting the troops in order, which certainly presents difficulties of exposition. This essay closely attends to the classic and its commentary, while its conception and diction are refined and dignified. By comparison, the superficial, ornate discussions of others only become more tiresome.”

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
同考試官編修趙批題本明易作者恒
務辭藻反失本旨求其語簡意足者無踰此
篇
同考試官編修黃批文武於德業非偏
也周公特各舉其盛者欲成王振德威服遠
以覲揚之意甚明而詞難遣士子甚為所窘
此作發揮從容若無難者宜錄之
考試官學士毛批用文武事入講讀之
不覺艱澁蓋善作者
===
考試官大學士梁批場屋寸晷中能具寫
周公告戒成王深意如此蓋亦不易得矣
先德顯于天下先業振于天下大臣望其君然
也甚矣先王之德之盛而業之大也自非後王
廣德威於天下其何以盡顯揚之責哉周公告
成王之意如此蓋謂有文事者必有武備承先
志者實惟後人彼德之小者不過一言一行之
善耳惟我文王以純亦不已之德光于四方顯
于西土其耿光蓋昭昭乎日月之照臨也今王

光德顯于天下光業振于天下大臣望其君然
也甚矣先王之德之盛而業之大也自非後王
廣德威於天下其何以盡顯揚之責哉周公告
成王之意如此蓋謂有文事者必有武備承先
志者實惟後人彼德之小者不過一言一行之
善耳惟我文王以純亦不已之德光于四方顯
于西土其耿光蓋昭昭乎日月之照臨也今王
punctuated:
同考試官編修趙批：題本明易，作者恒務辭藻，反失本旨。求其語簡意足者，無踰此篇。

同考試官編修黃批：文武於德業非偏也，周公特各舉其盛者，欲成王振德威、服遠以覲揚之，意甚明而詞難遣，士子甚為所窘。此作發揮從容，若無難者，宜錄之。

考試官學士毛批：用文武事入講，讀之不覺艱澁，蓋善作者。

考試官大學士梁批：場屋寸晷中，能具寫周公告戒成王深意如此，蓋亦不易得矣。

先德顯于天下，先業振于天下，大臣望其君然也。甚矣，先王之德之盛而業之大也！自非後王廣德威於天下，其何以盡顯揚之責哉？周公告成王之意如此。蓋謂有文事者必有武備，承先志者實惟後人。彼德之小者，不過一言一行之善耳。惟我文王以純亦不已之德，光于四方，顯于西土，其耿光蓋昭昭乎日月之照臨也。今王
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Hanlin Compiler: The topic is inherently clear and straightforward, yet writers habitually strive for ornate diction and thereby lose its essential meaning. For concise wording that fully conveys the sense, no essay surpasses this one.

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Hanlin Compiler: Kings Wen and Wu were not one-sided in their virtue and achievements. The Duke of Zhou merely singled out what was most eminent in each, wishing King Cheng to display his virtue and awe-inspiring might and bring distant peoples into submission, thereby making his predecessors’ greatness manifest and extolling it. The meaning is very clear, but finding the words to express it is difficult, and candidates are much hampered by this. This essay develops the meaning with ease, as though there were no difficulty. It deserves to be recorded.

Comment by Examiner Mao, Academician: The writer brings the deeds of Kings Wen and Wu into the exposition without making the reading feel labored or obscure. He is indeed an accomplished writer.

Comment by Examiner Liang, Grand Secretary: To set forth so fully the profound meaning of the Duke of Zhou’s admonition to King Cheng, within the brief time available in the examination hall, is indeed a rare accomplishment.

That the virtue of former rulers should be made manifest throughout the realm, and their achievements given renewed force throughout the realm—this is what a great minister expects of his ruler. How abundant was the virtue of the former kings, and how great their achievements! Unless their successor extends his virtue and awe-inspiring might throughout the realm, how can he fully discharge his responsibility to make their greatness manifest and extol it? Such was the intent of the Duke of Zhou’s admonition to King Cheng. For those who undertake civil affairs must also maintain military preparedness, and it is precisely those who come after who must carry on their predecessors’ purposes. Lesser virtue amounts to no more than goodness in a single word or deed. Our King Wen alone, through virtue that was pure and unceasing, shone upon the four quarters and made his greatness manifest in the western lands. His brilliant radiance was as resplendent as the illuminating sun and moon. Now Your Majesty…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
為文孫果能克詰戎兵使德威無地而弗屆則
皇風宣布人人衣被其光不異厥邦之時叙文
教休明在在會歸其極庶幾有夏之脩和光四
方者丕冒于無外鵲巢之化將快覩于重熈之
際也顯西土者覃被于無疆騶虞之詠將迭見
于繼統之餘也文王之德何有于遏佚哉彼功
之狹者不過一人一事之治耳惟我武王舉順
天應人之師永清四海萬姓悅服其大烈蓋蕩
蕩乎天地之覆載也今王為文子果能聿脩武
===
備使威德無遠而不服則安民之勇於今益顯
無委靡不振之虞敷賁之勢于昔愈張無削弱
不競之患海宇清寧奠洪基于不拔遠績自是
而輝煌也黎元愛戴保令緒于維新神功自是
而宏大也武王之業何有於陵替哉是則文王
非無業也以德言之則尤盛武王非無德也以
業言之則尤大是宜嗣王所宜覲揚之以求無
負於前人者歟嗟夫有周王業之成厥惟艱哉
成王繼之徒席安平廢武事吾恐怠玩以弛而

…as his illustrious grandson, if you can indeed put the troops and weapons in good order, so that your virtue and might reach everywhere, then the august influence will spread abroad, and everyone will be clothed in its radiance, just as when his own realm was duly ordered. Civil instruction will flourish brightly, and everywhere people will converge upon its highest standard, approaching the cultivated harmony of the central lands. The virtue that illuminated the four quarters will extend its great shelter everywhere, with nothing beyond it: the transforming influence celebrated in “The Magpie’s Nest” (Que chao) will then be witnessed with delight in an age of renewed prosperity. The virtue manifested in the western lands will spread without limit: praises like those in “The Zouyu” will appear repeatedly after the succession to the throne. How could King Wen’s virtue ever be checked or lost?

Those whose achievements are narrow accomplish no more than putting one person or one affair in order. Our King Wu alone raised an army that accorded with Heaven and answered the people’s wishes, bringing lasting peace to all within the four seas, so that the myriad families submitted joyfully. His great achievement was indeed as vast as Heaven’s covering and Earth’s bearing of all things. Now, as his illustrious son, if you can indeed cultivate military preparedness, so that no place is too distant to submit to your might and virtue, then the courage that brought peace to the people will become still more manifest today, without fear of languor or decline. The force of his widely displayed martial prowess will grow still greater than before, without danger of weakening or loss of strength. With the realm tranquil and peaceful, you will establish a great foundation that cannot be uprooted; his enduring accomplishments will thereby shine brilliantly. With the common people loving and supporting you, you will preserve his glorious legacy through continual renewal; his wondrous achievements will thereby become grand and far-reaching. How could King Wu’s undertaking ever fall into decline?

Thus King Wen was not without achievements, but his virtue was especially flourishing; King Wu was not without virtue, but his achievements were especially great. Surely these are what the succeeding king ought to display and exalt, seeking not to fail his predecessors! Alas, how difficult it was to establish the royal undertaking of Zhou! text:
陵遲之漸見矣顧能紹前休而大來裔哉况東
都之會以作六師則治安講武固先王所不廢
宜周公致意於斯也後乎召奭之告康王亦以
此為要務老臣謀國之忠類如此君天下者其

text:
仁則皆興仁上好讓則皆興讓而升猷之化於
是乎適成焉夫君之德固無俟乎羣黎百姓之
助也然民德既興行于下而君德益昭章于上
矣是豈非不助而助之也哉所謂平章百姓而
百姓昭明者是已羣黎百姓之象德亦非求所
以為事君也然民德既同歸於興行而君德益
隨之而廣被矣是豈非不為而為之也哉所謂
協和萬邦而黎民於變者是已神之詒福于我
君者有如是夫抑觀天保一詩前三章言天之
===
福其君後三章言神之福其君於天之福君者
則欲其如山阜岡陵而川至於神之福其君者
則欲其如日月南山與松柏皆臣子忠愛之至
情也豈非所謂上以是施之下以是報之者歟
千載而下讀其詩者猶藹然如在周廷見當時
君臣上下雍容相與之盛
价人維藩大師維垣大邦維屏大宗維翰
懷德維寧宗子維城
馬理

仁，則皆興仁；上好讓，則皆興讓，而升猷之化於是乎適成焉。夫君之德固無俟乎羣黎百姓之助也，然民德既興行于下，而君德益昭章于上矣。是豈非不助而助之也哉？所謂「平章百姓」而「百姓昭明」者，是已。羣黎百姓之象德，亦非求所以為事君也，然民德既同歸於興行，而君德益隨之而廣被矣。是豈非不為而為之也哉？所謂「協和萬邦」而「黎民於變」者，是已。神之詒福于我君者，有如是夫！抑觀《天保》一詩，前三章言天之福其君，後三章言神之福其君。於天之福君者，則欲其如山阜岡陵而川至；於神之福其君者，則欲其如日月南山與松柏。皆臣子忠愛之至情也，豈非所謂「上以是施之，下以是報之」者歟？千載而下，讀其詩者，猶藹然如在周廷，見當時君臣上下雍容相與之盛。

Associate Examiner Huang, Acting Vice Director, comments: The poet of “Perversity” (Ban), in his everyday admonitions to his colleagues, earnestly spoke of the great affairs of state, still fearing that he had not said enough. To treat one’s colleagues thus may indeed be called giving one’s utmost. This essay is rigorous in expression and correct in meaning, grasping the original purport deeply. Its concluding passage is especially effective in bringing out what the poet left unsaid. Ah! Can you be someone who merely knows how to speak?

Associate Examiner Wang, Supervising Secretary, comments: The topic itself is dignified, yet writers often fail to explain it clearly: their treatments are either prolix or vague, with no understanding of where the emphasis lies. A writer whose words are as concise and whose meaning is as complete as in this essay can hardly be regarded as an ordinary student of the Classics.

Associate Examiner Xu, Hanlin Compiler, comments: To place the ultimate emphasis on the ruler’s virtue is the poet’s profound intention. His interweaving of these statements is precisely the proper manner of indirectly admonishing a ruler, and you have brought this out. Moreover, your language and tone are mature; you must be no ordinary scholar.

text:
通篇皆妙佳士也
考試官大學士梁批快讀至終篇猶似有不
能盡言之意盖士之有素蘊者故以此取之
觀詩人取譬之意惟欲求多助於人而反求其
本於己也盖己德既修則多助自至為國者亦
求其本而已而奚以他求為哉詩人以是責同
列其憂時感事之意深矣是詩說者謂亦同列
相戒而作然責之之詞益又深切盖欲其諷達
於王也意謂人君之有天下其出治雖由於一
===
人而多助必資于羣力且以宮室焉譬之宮墻
之外有藩焉所以衛内垣而遠外患者也君之
价人其大德可以輔時其雅望可以鎮俗豈非
國之藩乎藩籬之内有垣焉所以固宮室而衛
内外者也君之大師居而為比閭族黨之民出
而為行伍軍師之衆豈非國之垣乎設之於門
以蔽内外者屏也而大邦之諸侯世守封疆奠
吾方岳為國之屏者其不在是乎百堵之墻所
恃以立者翰也而大宗之世冑族大以蕃義同

觀詩人取譬之意，惟欲求多助於人，而反求其本於己也。盖己德既修，則多助自至。為國者亦求其本而已，而奚以他求為哉？詩人以是責同列，其憂時感事之意深矣。是詩，說者謂亦同列相戒而作，然責之之詞益又深切，盖欲其諷達於王也。意謂人君之有天下，其出治雖由於一人，而多助必資于羣力。且以宮室焉譬之：宮墻之外有藩焉，所以衛内垣而遠外患者也。君之价人，其大德可以輔時，其雅望可以鎮俗，豈非國之藩乎？藩籬之内有垣焉，所以固宮室而衛内外者也。君之大師，居而為比閭族黨之民，出而為行伍軍師之衆，豈非國之垣乎？設之於門以蔽内外者，屏也。而大邦之諸侯，世守封疆，奠吾方岳，為國之屏者，其不在是乎？百堵之墻所恃以立者，翰也。而大宗之世冑，族大以蕃，義同
translation_en:
…The entire composition is excellent. This is a fine scholar.
Examiner Liang, Grand Secretary, comments: I read eagerly through to the end, yet there still seems to be more that he cannot fully express. He is evidently a scholar with a store of learning long cultivated; therefore I selected him on the strength of this composition.
Considering the poet’s intention in choosing these comparisons, he wishes only to seek abundant assistance from others, while turning back to seek its foundation in oneself. For once one has cultivated one’s own virtue, abundant assistance comes of itself. One who governs a state need only seek this foundation; why seek anything else? The poet uses this to admonish his colleagues: profound indeed is his concern for the times and his response to events. Commentators say that this poem, too, was composed as an admonition among colleagues. Yet its words of reproach are all the more earnest and searching, evidently because the poet wished his indirect remonstrance to reach the king. His meaning is that, when a ruler possesses all under Heaven, although the conduct of government proceeds from one man, abundant assistance must depend upon the strength of the many.
Take a palace as a comparison. Outside its walls stands a fence, which protects the inner walls and keeps external dangers at a distance. The ruler’s worthy men, whose great virtue can sustain the age and whose lofty reputation can steady popular customs—are they not the state’s fence? Inside the fence stand walls, which secure the palace and provide protection within and without. The ruler’s great multitude, who at home constitute the people organized into neighborhood groups and communities, and when mobilized constitute the ranks and units of the army—are they not the state’s walls? What is placed at the gate to screen the inside from the outside is a screen-wall. The lords of the great domains guard their territories from generation to generation and secure our regions: does not the state’s screen-wall lie in these men? What the hundred sections of wall depend upon to stand are their supporting posts. And the hereditary descendants of the great lineages, whose clans are large and flourishing, united in duty…

text:
休戚為國之翰者其不在茲乎夫藩垣屏翰安
之在人而可恃者也以德懷人安之在我而可
恃者也一德既修多助自至欲求安國之本舍
德其何以哉若夫宗子之城其安之可恃尤有
出于藩垣屏蔽之外者彼其以同姓之親為宗
人之子或系出文穆武昭之後或派別後王支
庶之家是雖無百雉之形而隱爾有金湯之重
其所繫信匪輕也又烏可不懷之以德以求其
鞏固之助也哉是則詩人之戒同列既惓惓上
===
及於國事而又要其歸於君德其憂深思遠之
意如此豈非欲因其友以達獻替之誠也哉抑
詩人於此既以國事及君德為言至於下章又
惓惓以敬天之怒為言而畧無一語及其朋友
相與之意者豈同列相戒之詞其義固如是哉
盖人臣愛君之心無有窮已平日有所聞見或
心所隱憂者義固當自言之於上如或勢位懸
隔不能以自達故猶欲為其同列之知己而得
言者深言之庶幾萬一獲見取而見聽焉是亦

translation_en:
…sharing weal and woe: are not those who serve as the state's supporting timbers to be found here? Protective fences, walls, screens, and supporting timbers are dependable means of security that lie in others; winning people over through virtue is a dependable means of security that lies in oneself. Once one's virtue is cultivated, abundant assistance comes of its own accord. If one seeks the foundation for securing the state, what means can there be apart from virtue?

As for the bulwark formed by the sons of the ruling lineage, the security on which one can rely extends still further than that afforded by protective fences, walls, and screens. These are kinsmen of the same surname, sons of the royal clan: some descend from the Mu line of King Wen and the Zhao line of King Wu; others branch off from the collateral houses of later kings. Though they have no physical form like a city wall a hundred zhi in circuit, they possess the unseen strength of metal ramparts and boiling moats. What depends upon them is certainly no slight matter. How, then, could one fail to win them over through virtue, so as to obtain their help in making the state secure?

Thus, in admonishing his colleagues, the poet earnestly raises his concerns to affairs of state and further insists that these ultimately rest upon the ruler's virtue. Such is the depth of his concern and the reach of his thought. Was he not seeking, through his friends, to convey his sincere wish to commend what is good and correct what is wrong? Yet here the poet speaks of affairs of state and the ruler's virtue, and in the following stanza he again speaks earnestly of revering Heaven's wrath, without so much as a single word about the mutual regard of friends. Can it be that this is precisely the proper meaning of words by which colleagues admonish one another?

A minister's love for his ruler indeed knows no end. Whatever he ordinarily hears or sees, or whatever causes him unspoken anxiety, duty requires that he report it personally to his sovereign. If, however, the distance between their positions prevents him from conveying it himself, he still wishes to speak fully of it to a trusted colleague who has the opportunity to address the ruler, hoping that there may be even the slightest chance that his counsel will be accepted and heard. This too is…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
見人君之政者夫人君與天地參以其心與政
也春秋立法垂訓其欲體元而合德也哉且夫
春秋表年紀事之書則凡即位而書一年可也
今魯隱嗣世不曰一年而謂之元年者何明人
君體元之心也盖以元即仁仁即心也人君之
元惟其心爾故正一心以及於朝廷正百官以
及於遠近是盖脗合乎太和之妙而默契乎含
弘之功也若然則乾元資始坤元資生運之財
成輔相而無遺人君之心其天地之心乎使春
===
秋止書一年則受終易代之義雖明記久明遠
之法雖立而人君之心不明於後世矣書曰月
正元日又曰元祀十有二月帝王之法然也春
秋述之而書元年之義有如此者若夫春秋事
以時成之例則凡無事而畧時月可也今魯隱
六年無事而書秋七月者何見人君合德之政
也盖以德惟政政在民也人君之德視其政爾
故春夏迭運而慶賞丕承秋冬代一行而兵刑祗
若是盖協賛乎元亨之機而潜孚乎利貞之用
