punctuated: 見人君之政者。夫人君與天地參，以其心與政也。《春秋》立法垂訓，其欲體元而合德也哉！且夫《春秋》，表年紀事之書，則凡即位而書一年可也。今魯隱嗣世，不曰一年而謂之元年者，何？明人君體元之心也。盖以元即仁，仁即心也。人君之元，惟其心爾。故正一心以及於朝廷，正百官以及於遠近，是盖脗合乎太和之妙，而默契乎含弘之功也。若然，則乾元資始、坤元資生，運之財成輔相而無遺，人君之心，其天地之心乎！使《春秋》止書一年，則受終易代之義雖明，記久明遠之法雖立，而人君之心不明於後世矣。《書》曰：「月正元日。」又曰：「元祀十有二月。」帝王之法然也。《春秋》述之，而書元年之義有如此者。若夫《春秋》事以時成之例，則凡無事而畧時月可也。今魯隱六年，無事而書秋七月者，何？見人君合德之政也。盖以德惟政，政在民也。人君之德，視其政爾。故春夏迭運而慶賞丕承，秋冬代一行而兵刑祗若，是盖協賛乎元亨之機，而潜孚乎利貞之用，
translation_en: …reveal the ruler’s governance. The ruler stands alongside Heaven and Earth by virtue of his heart and his governance. In establishing rules and transmitting instruction, did the Spring and Autumn Annals not intend that he embody the primal beginning and accord with their virtue? Now, the Spring and Autumn Annals is a book that marks years and records events, so whenever a ruler accedes, it would suffice to write “year one.” Why, then, when Duke Yin of Lu succeeded to the rulership, does it call this the “inaugural year” (yuan nian) rather than “year one”? It makes manifest the ruler’s heart that embodies the primal beginning. For the primal beginning is benevolence, and benevolence is the heart. The ruler’s primal beginning is simply his heart. Thus he rectifies his own heart and extends this rectitude to the court; he rectifies the hundred officials and extends this rectitude to those far and near. This accords with the subtle workings of supreme harmony and tacitly corresponds to the achievement of embracing and encompassing all things. If so, then the primal power of Qian, from which things take their beginning, and the primal power of Kun, from which things receive life, are put into operation through his ordering, completing, assisting, and supporting their work, with nothing omitted. Is the ruler’s heart not then the heart of Heaven and Earth? If the Spring and Autumn Annals wrote only “year one,” then, although the meaning of receiving the succession and changing reigns would be clear, and a method of recording long spans and making distant times intelligible would be established, the ruler’s heart would not be made manifest to later generations. The Book of Documents says, “On the first day of the first month,” and elsewhere, “In the twelfth month of the inaugural year.” Such was the practice of the emperors and kings. The Spring and Autumn Annals transmits it, and such is the significance of its writing “inaugural year.” As for the convention in the Spring and Autumn Annals whereby events are completed through the recording of their seasons, it would suffice to omit the season and month whenever nothing happened. Why, then, in Duke Yin of Lu’s sixth year, when nothing happened, does it write “Autumn, seventh month”? It reveals the ruler’s governance that accords with the virtue of Heaven and Earth. For virtue consists in governance, and governance concerns the people. The ruler’s virtue is to be judged simply by his governance. Thus, as spring and summer move in succession, celebrations and rewards grandly carry forward their work; as autumn and winter take their successive course [?], military action and punishments reverently follow theirs. This assists the workings of origination and flourishing, and inwardly accords with the operation of benefit and steadfastness…

===

以專之者而況禮莫大於分乎故惟有宗伯以
命國有司馬以出師而後臣節安矣僖也征討
之禁未聞封建之制未請徒以母氏之言可奉

考試官學士毛批：得胡傳意，而文字有筆力，盖他卷所無。
考試官大學士梁批：三場皆明暢，此作尤能發明所以書取、書及之意，故取之以冠本房。
春秋於望國，因用兵而著專王命之罪，因交兵而著輕民命之罪。此須句之復書曰取，升陘之戰不言公而書及也。春秋之罪魯者有以哉！且須句，風姓，實司皞濟之祀，君嘗以邾滅奔魯矣。魯僖憫之，整伐邾之旅，為復國之圖焉。人曰：須句見復，得崇祀保小之禮也。君子何以為譏？盖威福大柄，王命之所出也。雖禮所得為，亦不可以專之者，而況禮莫大於分乎？故惟有宗伯以命國，有司馬以出師，而後臣節安矣。僖也，征討之禁未聞，封建之制未請，徒以母氏之言可奉
translation_en:
…The writings produced in the examination hall are generally superficial, verbose, and one-sided. Moreover, they pile up words and phrases into parallel prose, failing to grasp the Sage’s intention in condemning Lu. This essay presents its account neatly and delivers judgments with concision and rigor. Its language is economical, yet its meaning is complete. Recording it here may also help eliminate the faults prevalent today.
Comment by Examiner Mao, Academician: It captures the meaning of Hu’s Commentary, and its writing has a force lacking in the other scripts.
Comment by Examiner Liang, Grand Secretary: The work in all three sessions is clear and fluent. This piece is especially successful in elucidating the intention behind writing “took” and “and.” I have therefore selected it to head the scripts from this examining room.
In its treatment of Wang [?], the Spring and Autumn Annals exposes, through the use of military force, the offense of arrogating royal authority; through armed engagements, it exposes the offense of treating the people’s lives lightly. This is why the restoration of Xuju is recorded as “took,” and why the battle of Shengxing is recorded with “and,” without mentioning the duke. The Spring and Autumn Annals has good reason to condemn Lu!
Now Xuju, whose ruling house bore the surname Feng, was responsible for the sacrifices to Hao and the Ji River. Its ruler had previously fled to Lu when Zhu destroyed his state. Duke Xi of Lu pitied him, mustered troops to attack Zhu, and planned to restore his state. People say: “The restoration of Xuju accorded with the ritual principles of honoring sacrifices and protecting small states.” Why, then, does the gentleman regard it as blameworthy? The great powers of punishment and reward belong to the authority from which royal commands issue. Even what ritual permits must not be undertaken on one’s own authority. Moreover, what is more important in ritual than the distinctions of rank? Thus, only when the Minister of Rites authorizes the establishment of states and the Minister of War dispatches armies can the proper bounds of a subject’s conduct remain secure. Yet Duke Xi had not heeded the prohibition against unauthorized punitive expeditions, nor requested authorization for enfeoffment; he merely took his mother’s words as something to be obeyed…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
也若然則歳功維叙乾道乃革者之對時育物
而不謬人君之政其四時之政乎使春秋畧是
時月則一時不具而歳功虧一德不備而乾道
熄人君之政不見於後世矣易曰乾元亨利貞
又曰君子行此四德者天人之理然也春秋一
之而書秋七月之義有如此者噫元者天地之
用也而人君體之德者四時之運也而人君合
之則天地之用不在元而在君之心四時之運
不在德而在君之政矣雖然政者心之用也心
===
正則政罔弗臧猶四德並行而乾元以統天耳
此又春秋託始之微意人君其念之哉

translation_en:
…so. If this is so, the year's work proceeds in due order; the Way of Qian is then transformed, responding to the seasons and nurturing things without error [?]. Is not the ruler's government a government patterned upon the four seasons? If the Spring and Autumn Annals omitted these seasons and months, one season would be missing and the year's work impaired; one virtue would be lacking and the Way of Qian extinguished. The ruler's government would no longer be visible to later ages. The Book of Changes says: “Qian: origination, fulfillment, benefit, and steadfastness.” It also says: “The gentleman practices these four virtues.” Such is the principle governing Heaven and humanity. The Spring and Autumn Annals unites them, and such is the significance of its recording “autumn, the seventh month.” Ah! Origination is the operation of Heaven and Earth, and the ruler embodies it; virtue is the movement of the four seasons, and the ruler accords with it. Thus the operation of Heaven and Earth resides not in origination but in the ruler's heart; the movement of the four seasons resides not in virtue but in the ruler's government. Nevertheless, government is the functioning of the heart. If the heart is upright, nothing in government will fail to be good, just as the four virtues operate together while Qian's origination governs Heaven. This, too, is the subtle intent of the beginning established by the Spring and Autumn Annals. Let rulers ponder it!
“In spring, the duke attacked Zhu and took Xuju. In autumn, on the dingwei day of the eighth month, [our forces] fought the men of Zhu at Shengxing.” Both entries are from the twenty-second year of Duke Xi.
Tang Gao.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Compiler: The classic and its commentary are very clear on this topic, but…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
也而擅行之於邾有報母怨之私於須句則有
專置之僭是與爭奪者一爾而豈所以為禮哉
春秋貶之故不言復而書取其尊王命也如此
若邾婁附庸嘗覆須句之祀今又以魯憾出師
矣魯僖卑之忽戰守之備有升陘之敗焉人曰
魯師雖敗由誅暴禁亂之義也君子何以為諱
盖兵戎大事民命之所繫也雖義所得用亦不
可以輕之者而況義則不以力乎故善為國者
不師善師者不陣而後君德全矣僖也文告之
===
詞未修疆場之守無備雖有賢臣之言弗用也
而輕禦之在魯有獲公冑之危在邾人亦有復
矢之憯是與暴亂者一爾而豈可以為義哉春
秋貶之故不言公而書及其重民命也如此吁
尊王命則統體一而大分嚴重民命則禍亂熄
而大本固垂訓之義亦精矣乎抑魯僖賢侯其
見於頌可考也而晚年之行類如此豈其時宋
襄繼齊桓之盛文仲非季友之賢而無疆之思
固無以勝怠荒之志邪噫此有國者存內外之

translation_en:
… Yet he acted on his own authority against Zhu, privately seeking to avenge his mother’s grievance; in Xuju, he presumptuously installed a ruler on his own authority. In this he was no different from those who contend for conquest. How could this constitute ritual propriety? The Spring and Autumn Annals censures him: hence it does not say “restored,” but records “took.” Such is its reverence for the king’s commands.

As for Zhulou, a dependent state, it had once extinguished the ancestral sacrifices of Xuju, and now again sent out troops because of its grievance against Lu. Duke Xi of Lu despised it and neglected preparations for battle and defense, suffering defeat at Shengxing. Someone might say: “Although Lu’s army was defeated, it acted on the righteous principle of punishing violence and suppressing disorder. Why should the gentleman conceal this?” Military action is a grave matter upon which the people’s lives depend. Even when righteousness permits its use, it must not be undertaken lightly. How much more so when righteousness should prevail without force! Thus, one skilled in governing a state does not resort to armies; one skilled in employing armies does not draw them up for battle. Only then is a ruler’s virtue complete.

Duke Xi had not prepared the language of his formal proclamations, and his frontier defenses were unready. Though a worthy minister offered counsel, he did not heed it, but rashly resisted the enemy. On Lu’s side, there was the peril in which the duke’s helmet was captured; on the side of the men of Zhu, there was also the cruelty of returning the arrows [?]. In this he was no different from the violent and disorderly. How could this be considered righteous? The Spring and Autumn Annals censures him: hence it does not name “the duke,” but records “engaged with.” Such is its concern for the people’s lives.

Ah! When the king’s commands are honored, the governing order is unified and the great distinctions of rank are strictly maintained. When the people’s lives are valued, calamity and disorder cease, and the great foundation is secure. How profound are the principles by which it transmits instruction! Yet Duke Xi of Lu was a worthy lord, as can be verified from his portrayal in the Hymns. Why, then, were his later actions of this sort? Was it because Duke Xiang of Song had succeeded to Duke Huan of Qi’s ascendancy, while Wenzhong lacked Jiyou’s worthiness, so that thoughts extending without limit could not overcome an inclination toward indolence and neglect? Alas! Here those who possess a state must attend to internal and external …

Book of Rites
“When virtue is perfected, instruction is honored; when instruction is honored, officials are upright; when officials are upright, the state is well governed.”

text:
修內外之教而性之成於世子者恭敬而溫文
師保嚴翼賛之勤而道之喻於世子者孝慈而
忠敬德成如此則是其君國之本已備於其未
君國之先吾知德明惟明時而出也豈不足以
範人而立極德威惟畏時而發也自皆足以作
則而立威德以預養而成教即由德而立矣教
不尊邪教尊則官者所以承其教者也其孰有
不正者乎極建於此而觀者感焉自將懋德交
修而對揚乎光訓大臣法小臣廉所謂庶尹允
===
諧弗誣上而行私矣官正則國者又所以理於
官者也其復有不治者乎化行於近而遠者則
焉自將敷言錫保而允升于大猷父子篤兄弟
睦所謂下民祗協弗背德而作奸矣吁上下之
化本於其德成於世子之時如此世子其可以
不預養哉抑嘗攷三王盛時莫不以預養世子
為首務盖世子天下本也故曰世子生而固舉
以禮生斯教也長就師保禮樂倫理教無不備
惰慢邪僻防無不周其所以預養之者如此故

His preceptors and guardians attend rigorously to their diligent assistance, so that the Way made clear to the heir apparent consists in filial devotion, parental kindness, loyalty, and reverence. With his virtue thus perfected, the foundation for governing his state is already complete before he begins to rule. I know that the brilliance of his virtue is truly illuminating: when manifested at the proper time, how could it fail to provide a pattern for others and establish the highest standard? The majesty of his virtue is truly awe-inspiring: when displayed at the proper time, it will assuredly suffice to establish a model and inspire awe. Virtue is perfected through cultivation in advance, and his teaching is then established through that virtue. Will his teaching not command respect?

When his teaching commands respect, the officials are those who receive and carry it out. Which of them could fail to be upright? This is what is meant by “the many officers are truly harmonious”: they will not deceive their superiors and pursue private interests. Once the officials are upright, the state, in turn, is governed through them. How could it then fail to be well governed? His transforming influence operates nearby, and those far away take it as their model. They will naturally disseminate his words, bestow protection, and truly advance toward the great Way. Fathers and sons will be devoted, and brothers harmonious. This is what is meant by “the common people reverently cooperate”: they will not turn their backs on virtue and commit wrongdoing.

聞然猶不自信也質之衆言之所同者斯守之

…it is insufficient to encompass all the good words in the world. The gentleman therefore seeks them out, leaving none unheard; yet he still does not trust his own judgment. He tests them against what the words of others hold in common, and then preserves them in his heart without losing them. How discerning he is! Without remembering much, one cannot assemble all the good deeds in the world. The gentleman therefore observes them, leaving none unremembered; yet he still does not assume that he is right. He tests them against what the deeds of others hold in common, and then tirelessly practices them himself [?]. How discerning he is! Such is what is meant by being careless in nothing concerning knowledge. Yet could this be merely a matter of knowing?

The ruler expects to consult his ministers about assisting in affairs and ordering the various categories of business [?]; the minister’s duty is to repay him by winning support and attachment, and by diligently carrying out his service. This necessarily entails action. Can one act without seeking what is essential? Thus, after arriving at understanding through selection and discrimination, one must again scrutinize matters carefully at the very inception of thought. Only when a thought accords with righteousness does one give it expression and act upon it, whether to assist the ruler or to extend its benefits to the people. In transmitting counsel upward and commands downward, one must be trustworthy: this requires only simplicity. Why? Because righteousness, when unified, is naturally simple. Only when an initiative accords with the Way does one put it forth and act upon it, whether to propagate illustrious instructions or to advance the sovereign’s work. What those above and below share requires only concision. Why? Because the Way, at its fullest realization, is naturally concise. Such is what is meant by being careless in nothing concerning action.

Ah! Is this why his words and deeds are all good, and his integrity cannot be wrested from him? Yet consider what the preceding passage says: “When one below serves one above, if his person is not upright and his words are not trustworthy, his righteousness will lack unity and his conduct will lack consistency. The righteous relationship between ruler and minister is the constant order of Heaven and the guiding principle of Earth. If a gentleman devotes himself to learning, how could he still lack integrity? The sage was concerned…

同考試官編修景批：議論多而不事起伏，氣格大而不事激發，言詞富而盡去夫刻削奇麗之病，而結束數語尤見體驗。是盖有得於傳心之學者歟？

考試官學士毛批：論得延平意，雖不求異而造語自新，且文勢抑揚高下間俱入法度，殆所謂粹温中有奇氣者歟？

考試官大學士梁批：不求奇崛，只就延平本語而發揮之，故自可觀。場屋文字當如是也。

論曰：聖賢之相授受，亦惟其有卓然不易之見
translation_en:
…to replace corruption with corruption leaves little difference. This composition on the transmission of the mind [?] grounds its language in principle and abounds in vital force, seeming to possess reserves that cannot be exhausted. Its author’s talent and discernment far surpass those of others.

Associate Examiner Jing, Senior Compiler, comments: Its arguments are abundant, yet it does not contrive rises and falls; its force and stature are great, yet it does not strive for heightened effects. Its language is rich, yet entirely free of the faults of over-refinement and exotic ornament. The few concluding sentences especially reveal understanding gained through personal practice. Surely this is someone who has attained something in the learning of the transmission of the mind?

Associate Examiner Li, Senior Compiler, comments: Candidates writing discourses strive for elaborate refinement, even to the point of making their work unreadable. They call it ancient-style prose, unaware that the true meaning is instead obscured. This essay alone examines its subject repeatedly over several hundred words and explains the principles clearly and fully. Moreover, its talent is outstanding and its spirit untrammeled; these qualities certainly do not detract from its literary accomplishment.

Examiner Mao, Academician, comments: The discourse captures Yanping’s meaning. Although it does not seek novelty, its expressions are naturally fresh. Moreover, throughout the rising and falling movement of its prose, everything accords with proper standards. Is this not what is meant by extraordinary vitality within purity and warmth?

Examiner Liang, Grand Secretary, comments: It does not seek startling originality, but simply develops Yanping’s own words, and thus naturally merits attention. Examination writing ought to be like this.

The discourse reads: What sages and worthies transmit to one another consists simply in their possessing an understanding that stands firmly and does not change…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
而又有俛焉不已之學而已夫天地之生久矣
其治亂窮通之數常相尋於無窮是固决有非
人力所能改移者聖賢於此其獨且奈之何哉
亦惟一委之于命焉耳然而於吾身心當然之
理凡所以學之于己而不敢不盡者則未嘗一
日而不加之意也嗚呼兹聖賢之所以默相傳
授之心法而延平李氏之所以超然獨得而留
以遺教于後學者歟請得而推之今夫天下盖
不能以皆治也亦或有否之之時者矣不能以
===
皆通也亦或有窮之之時者矣是皆氣化之互
相推移人事之迭為倚伏固有不能以必其一
律齊者聖賢于此亦獨何為也哉其必曰責之
己而不敢責之天盡其所當然之理而不敢較
其所不必然之數云耳况樂治而厭亂喜通而
惡窮雖聖賢之心亦不能以異于人顧其心之
所以處之者實非人之所能及也自今言之身
繫綱常倫理之重不可以不愛也吾惟知愛吾
身而已耳其於身之或窮或通或禍或福吾不

translation_en:
…and also possess a diligence in learning that never ceases. Heaven and earth have existed for a long time. The allotted cycles of order and disorder, adversity and success, continually follow one another without end; among these there are assuredly things that human effort cannot alter. What, then, can even sages and worthies do about them? They can only entrust them wholly to fate. Yet concerning the principles that ought to govern their own persons and minds—all that they must learn and realize within themselves, and dare not leave unfulfilled—they never pass a single day without attending to them. Ah! Is this not the method of cultivating the mind that sages and worthies silently transmitted to one another, and that Master Li of Yanping grasped with exceptional insight and left as instruction for later students? Allow me to develop this further.

The world cannot always enjoy order: there are also times of obstruction. Nor can it always enjoy success: there are also times of adversity. These all arise from the alternating transformations of vital energy and the vicissitudes of human affairs, in which one condition harbors the possibility of its opposite. They assuredly cannot be made uniformly the same. What, then, can sages and worthies do about them? They must say only: demand fulfillment of oneself, without daring to demand it of Heaven; fully realize the principles of what ought to be, without daring to contest the allotments of what need not necessarily come to pass. Moreover, even sages and worthies cannot differ from other people in delighting in order and loathing disorder, welcoming success and hating adversity. Yet the way their minds respond to these conditions is truly beyond the reach of others.

To speak of this now: one's person bears the weight of the cardinal bonds, constant virtues, and ethical relationships, and therefore must be cherished. I know only to cherish my person. As for whether my person encounters adversity or success, calamity or good fortune, I do not…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
得而知也道為萬化萬事之源不可以不明也
吾惟知明吾道而已耳美於道之或顯或晦或
行或否吾不得而知也己負家國天下之責不
可以不修也吾惟知修吾己以俟時而已耳其
於時之我遇我乖我否我泰吾不得而知也若
是者豈聖賢故為是勞以自取異于天下後世
也哉蓋治也亂也窮也通也有天者寓乎其間
而非人之所能與愛身也明道也修己俟時也
皆吾力之所能為而非天之所可變可變則非
===
聖賢矣故所遭而治而通則心之所以處之者
固所以處亂處窮之道也所遭而亂而窮則心
之所以處之者固所以處治處通之道也嗚呼
此古聖賢卓然之見俛焉之學所以默相授受
於數千百載之間者其道固如是耳蓋嘗觀諸
舜矣自塗廩浚井之時以至攝政格祖之際而
所以守之者何如也又嘗觀諸周公矣自跋胡
疐尾之日以至反風偃禾之餘而所以守之者
何如也繼周公者孔子也阨于陳蔡之間仕于

得而知也。道為萬化萬事之源，不可以不明也。吾惟知明吾道而已耳，美於道之或顯或晦、或行或否，吾不得而知也。己負家國天下之責，不可以不修也。吾惟知修吾己以俟時而已耳，其於時之我遇我乖、我否我泰，吾不得而知也。若是者，豈聖賢故為是勞，以自取異于天下後世也哉？蓋治也、亂也、窮也、通也，有天者寓乎其間，而非人之所能與。愛身也、明道也、修己俟時也，皆吾力之所能為，而非天之所可變。可變，則非聖賢矣。故所遭而治而通，則心之所以處之者，固所以處亂處窮之道也；所遭而亂而窮，則心之所以處之者，固所以處治處通之道也。嗚呼！此古聖賢卓然之見、俛焉之學，所以默相授受於數千百載之間者，其道固如是耳。

translation_en:
…I cannot know. The Way is the source of all transformations and all affairs, and must be understood clearly. I know only to clarify my understanding of the Way. As for [?] whether the Way becomes manifest or obscure, whether it is put into practice or not, I cannot know. I bear responsibilities toward my family, the state, and all under Heaven, and must cultivate myself. I know only to cultivate myself and await the proper time. Whether the times will favor or thwart me, bring me adversity or prosperity, I cannot know. Is this because sages and worthies deliberately undertake such toil to distinguish themselves from everyone under Heaven and from later generations? Order and disorder, adversity and success all contain an element of Heaven’s working in which human beings cannot intervene. Cherishing oneself, illuminating the Way, and cultivating oneself while awaiting the proper time are all within one’s own power, and are things that Heaven cannot alter. If they could be altered, one would not be a sage or worthy. Thus, when they encounter order and success, the way their hearts respond is precisely the way to respond to disorder and adversity; when they encounter disorder and adversity, the way their hearts respond is precisely the way to respond to order and success. Ah! Such indeed is the Way embodied in the outstanding insight and diligent learning of the ancient sages and worthies, silently transmitted and received across hundreds and thousands of years.

I have considered this in the case of Shun. From the time he plastered the granary and deepened the well to the time he acted as regent and entered the ancestral temple, how did he hold fast to his principles? I have also considered this in the case of the Duke of Zhou. From the days when, like a wolf, he stumbled over his dewlap and tripped over his tail, to the aftermath of the wind’s reversal and the flattened grain, how did he hold fast to his principles? title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
定公之朝而當時固窮之對相事之攝不可見
其所守矣乎繼孔子者孟子也游于齊梁之邦
沮于臧倉之口而當時仁義之說義命之安不
可見其所守矣乎嗚呼之數聖賢者當其處治
處通處窮處亂之時而所以愛身所以明道所
以修已俟時之法固有一日不能忘焉者其在
周公猶其在舜也蓋舜以是心法而傳之周公
也其在孔子猶其在周公也蓋周公以是心法
而傳之孔子也其在孟子猶其在孔子也蓋孔
===
子以是心法而傳之孟子也舜也周公也孔子
也孟子也雖不必面相授受於一堂之上而此
心同此理同則其心法之傳固有不能以不同
焉者矣向使其於身心所當然之理一有未盡
則非上天所以生聖賢之意而天下後世之人
亦必將叢集而議其責噫則亦安在其為聖為
賢也哉然則聖賢傳心之要法其孰有加于是
者哉抑延平之言其殆有所為也乎當光孝之
朝國勢不振學禁方嚴而一時以儒自名者至

…at the court of Duke Ding. In his reply about remaining steadfast in adversity and his assumption of ministerial duties at that time, can we not see what he upheld? Mengzi succeeded Kongzi. He traveled in the states of Qi and Liang and was thwarted by Zang Cang’s words. In his teachings on benevolence and righteousness and his repose in righteousness and Heaven’s decree at that time, can we not see what he upheld? Alas! These several sages and worthies, whether living amid good government, enjoying success, enduring adversity, or facing disorder, possessed methods for preserving themselves, illuminating the Way, and cultivating themselves while awaiting their time that they could not forget for even a day. In the Duke of Zhou these were the same as in Shun, for Shun transmitted this method of cultivating the mind to the Duke of Zhou. In Kongzi they were the same as in the Duke of Zhou, for the Duke of Zhou transmitted this method to Kongzi. In Mengzi they were the same as in Kongzi, for Kongzi transmitted this method to Mengzi. Shun, the Duke of Zhou, Kongzi, and Mengzi need not have transmitted and received it face to face in a single hall: their minds were the same and their principles were the same, so the transmission of their method of cultivating the mind necessarily shared this sameness. Had they fallen short in any respect of the principles governing the proper conduct of body and mind, they would have failed Heaven’s purpose in bringing forth sages and worthies, and people throughout the world in later generations would surely have gathered to debate their culpability. Alas! In what, then, would their sageliness or worthiness have consisted? What essential method by which sages and worthies transmit the mind could surpass this?

Through a second transmission came Cai Yuanding, who, on his journey to Daozhou, went on foot to carry out his undertaking [?]. Thus the transmission of their method of cultivating the mind also had its source.

Nevertheless, in times of order and success, making this effort is easy; in days of disorder and adversity, it is difficult. What is easy, ordinary people may perhaps accomplish through exertion; what is difficult, none but sages and worthies can accomplish. Let me offer this to complete the meaning that Yanping left unexpressed.

Memorial

translation_en:
…The sage emperor examines antiquity, always grasping the essentials to govern the manifold; we, humble scholars compiling these sayings, likewise arrange them by category and bring related matters together. No sooner had we submitted the work for Your Majesty’s discerning inspection than you bestowed upon it an auspicious title. Now that its preface is complete, we venture once more to offer wishes celebrating your glory. We, your servants, earnestly reflect that the Way of Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang is like the sun shining in heaven, while the writings of Confucius, Zengzi, Zisi, and Mencius are like water flowing across the earth. Even the records of the various schools and histories are all extensions of the sages’ classics and the worthies’ commentaries. Yet if the selection is insufficiently discriminating, breadth of learning yields few essentials. Who can adjudicate the confusion of these many sayings? Surely this must await the manifold abilities of one who is truly a sage.

We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor is reverent and enlightened, profoundly wise, diligent and frugal, magnanimous and humane. In your own person you embody the harmonious influences of all four seasons; with a few words you penetrate the profound mysteries of all antiquity. You hold that, although the principles by which human beings establish themselves in this world and the sages and worthies transmit instruction to future generations have more than one aspect, their essentials truly reside in three matters. Only when the ruler is reverent, ministers loyal, and sons filial does moral transformation spread, customs flourish, and the people live in harmony; the bringing about of good government…

translation_en:
…the foundations of human harmony and orderly government all arise from this. Yet accounts of these matters are scattered throughout the classics and their commentaries, and consulting the texts still requires laborious investigation. Thus they have now been compiled into a book, to make them concise, clear, and readily accessible. Surely this is not merely to furnish reading for Your Majesty in the second watch of the night; it is intended to bequeath a standard for a hundred generations. You graciously wish to share with your descendants, officials, and people the sight of all Three Bonds being upheld, so that even the Rong, Yi, Man, and Mo peoples may behold every mesh of the net fully spread. Indeed, what is here elucidated accords with remotest antiquity and may await a sage yet to come without misgiving.
We, your servants, possess no talents suited to this task, and our learning has yet to find its proper direction. Reverently receiving your imperial command, we have bent to the work of writing and editing. Our compilation is inadequate, and we occupy in vain the office of Left Recorder. Though our exposition is prolix, how could it carry forward the purport of Bu Shang? We seek only to remain plain and straightforward, hoping not to disappoint the nurturing you have bestowed upon us. Beyond this, we do not know how to proceed. Looking up to Heaven and reverently regarding Your Sagely Majesty, we, your servants, cannot contain our intense emotion and trembling awe. We respectfully submit this memorial together with the work for your imperial attention.

First question.

Associate Examiner Huang, Acting Vice Director, comments: The magnificence of our Sagely Founder’s words and deeds, achievements, and institutions surpasses all antiquity. Even the records preserved in golden coffers and stone chambers cannot fully encompass it. This policy essay excels in setting it forth: concise yet omitting nothing, does it not show an exceptional grasp of what is most important? We record it for more than its literary merit alone.
Associate Examiner Wang, Supervising Secretary, comments: The magnificence of our Sagely Founder’s achievements, virtue, and institutions cannot readily be expressed in words. Candidates generally do no more than expand directly upon the question; those who occasionally identify a point or two still tend to cite minor matters and omit the major ones. This composition is accurate in its facts and fluent in its language, celebrating almost exhaustively the broad outlines and essential points. Is its author not one who has been most deeply nurtured by the sage influence?
Associate Examiner Xu, Hanlin Academy Compiler, comments: Our Sagely Founder’s virtue and achievements, like Yao’s, defy description. For later students even to glimpse them is already difficult; to expound and celebrate them is harder still. This essay manages to bring together his methods for promoting the Way and achieving good government, and the magnificence of his rites and music. Its several hundred flowing words extend throughout beyond the question’s stated scope. Such lofty aspirations and remarkable discernment—can these be merely literary accomplishments? In his response at the Palace Examination, he may have a further opportunity to expound and celebrate these matters and give full expression to his views. I await the chance to see it.

translation_en:
…the words, deeds, plans, and achievements of our Sacred Progenitor surpass those of all past ages, while all his imperially composed books arose from his personal practice and inward understanding. It is therefore quite wrong to seek to comprehend him through words and writings alone. This essay celebrates and extols him with the utmost detail and completeness. What is called “understanding the greater things”—I have seen this in you.
Associate Examiner Li, Right Mentor, comments: This policy essay celebrates almost exhaustively the magnificence of our Sacred Progenitor’s plans, instructions, accomplishments, and achievements. Moreover, it is dignified and mature, without striving for ornament. Its author is indeed a man of discernment. My respectful admiration! My respectful admiration!
Examiner Mao, Academician, comments: Our Imperial Progenitor’s excellent words, good deeds, plans, instructions, accomplishments, and achievements, together with all his imperially composed books, flowed from his learning of the mind. They truly suffice to carry forward the greatness of the ancient emperors and kings; all else scarcely merits mention. And now there has appeared a man such as this, capable of understanding these things deeply and extolling them! Ah, how could many such men be found?
Examiner Liang, Grand Secretary, comments: He does not narrowly concern himself with matching the particulars of the question. Yet the conclusion he reaches after his expansive praise remains consistent with its intent. He is indeed a man who understands words. Moreover, much in his other compositions is commendable; his selection for a high place is fitting.
I reverently consider that the magnificent virtue and great achievements of our Sacred Progenitor are like Heaven and Earth, which leave nothing uncovered or unsupported, and like the sun and moon…

translation_en:
…whose illumination reaches everywhere. Thus even the learned gentlemen of the age, reputed for their breadth of learning, cannot survey it all or comprehend it fully. How much less could a scholar from a humble dwelling, such as this ignorant student, be capable of knowing it? Nevertheless, dare I fail to set forth a few particulars in reply to your discerning question?

Alas, in former times the barbarian Yuan defiled our central land. The August Lord on High, mindful of the people below, brought forth our Sagely Founder to come forward and deliver them. He gave full scope to his gifts of intelligence and divine martial prowess, and handed down a tradition of centrality, rectitude, benevolence, and righteousness. He established fundamental principles and set out governing rules, instituted rites and created music. Through military achievement he pacified All under Heaven; through civil virtue he brought about Great Peace.

He attended court before dawn and, even late in the day, forgot to eat. With an open mind he sought clear counsel, accepting good advice as readily as water flows. He rejected extravagance and earnestly esteemed frugality. Within the palace, he strictly maintained the separation between the inner and outer quarters; authority showed no tendency to pass into subordinate hands. He established schools and advanced men of outstanding ability and virtue. He observed scrupulously the rites of the suburban sacrifices, the ancestral temple, and the altars of Soil and Grain, and put in proper order the sacrifices to the seas, sacred mountains, and myriad spirits. None outside the imperial lineage was made a prince; none without meritorious service was made a marquis. In the civil-service examinations he abolished the superficiality of ornate verse and rhapsodies; in popular customs he reformed the coarseness of barbarian practices.

He took no delight in such auspicious signs as sweet dew, felicitous clouds, and numinous fungi; but drought, solar eclipses, and anomalies among the stars filled him with apprehension. Though he promoted agriculture and military training, he constantly guarded against delighting in arms. Though harvests were plentiful and goods abundant, yet…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
猶以民勞為慮累行蠲租振貧褒忠表節
之政每斥獻諛言利巧文深詆之人議從
祀帝王之廟則去趙普而進潘美惡不忠
也議從祀孔廟之庭則去楊雄而進仲舒
惡仕莽也於故元見獲之子姓及其忠節
之舊臣或厚撫而送歸或褒嘉而秩祀於
四夷朝貢之君長與侯于周服之臣庶来
則懷之以示勸悖則威之以示懲其論治
道也則曰為治之道有緩急治亂民不可
===
急急之則益亂撫治民不可擾擾之則不
治故烹鮮之言雖小可以喻大治繩之說
雖淺可以喻深其論兵政也則曰人皆言
休兵偃武不知治兵始可以休兵講武始
可以偃武其論古人也則曰漢高帝從善
如不及唐太宗未免有矜功挾能之意楚
莊王謀事而當群臣莫及朝而有憂色魏
武侯與群臣謀事而當群臣莫及朝而有
喜色夫喜者矜其所長憂者憂其所不足

punctuated:
猶以民勞為慮，累行蠲租振貧、褒忠表節之政，每斥獻諛言利、巧文深詆之人。議從祀帝王之廟，則去趙普而進潘美，惡不忠也；議從祀孔廟之庭，則去楊雄而進仲舒，惡仕莽也。於故元見獲之子姓及其忠節之舊臣，或厚撫而送歸，或褒嘉而秩祀。於四夷朝貢之君長與侯于周服之臣庶，来則懷之以示勸，悖則威之以示懲。
其論治道也，則曰：「為治之道有緩急，治亂民不可急，急之則益亂；撫治民不可擾，擾之則不治。故烹鮮之言雖小，可以喻大；治繩之說雖淺，可以喻深。」
其論兵政也，則曰：「人皆言休兵偃武，不知治兵始可以休兵，講武始可以偃武。」
其論古人也，則曰：「漢高帝從善如不及，唐太宗未免有矜功挾能之意。楚莊王謀事而當，群臣莫及，朝而有憂色；魏武侯與群臣謀事而當，群臣莫及，朝而有喜色。夫喜者矜其所長，憂者憂其所不足。
translation_en:
…he nevertheless remained concerned about the people's toil. He repeatedly enacted measures to remit taxes, relieve the poor, commend loyalty, and honor steadfast integrity. He regularly rejected men who offered flattery, advocated profit, or manipulated written charges to incriminate others severely. When discussing associated worship in the temple of emperors and kings, he removed Zhao Pu and admitted Pan Mei, out of abhorrence for disloyalty. When discussing associated worship in the precincts of the Confucian temple, he removed Yang Xiong and admitted Zhongshu, out of abhorrence for service under Wang Mang. As for captured descendants of the former Yuan ruling house and its former ministers who had maintained their loyalty and integrity, he either treated them generously and sent them home, or commended them and accorded them a place in the prescribed sacrifices. As for the rulers and chieftains of the foreign peoples who presented tribute, together with subjects and commoners within the territories of allegiance [?], he cherished those who came, to encourage submission, and overawed those who rebelled, to demonstrate punishment.
Discussing the way of government, he said: “In governing, some matters require restraint and others urgency. One must not press a disorderly populace too hard: doing so only increases disorder. One must not disturb an orderly populace when tending to it: doing so destroys its order. Thus, although the saying about cooking small fish concerns something small, it can illustrate something great; although the explanation about putting cords in order is simple, it can illustrate something profound.”
Discussing military administration, he said: “Everyone speaks of resting the troops and laying down arms, without understanding that only by putting the army in order can one rest the troops, and only by practicing military skills can one lay down arms.”
Discussing the ancients, he said: “Emperor Gao of Han followed good counsel as though he could never do so quickly enough. Emperor Taizong of Tang was not entirely free of pride in his achievements and reliance on his abilities. When King Zhuang of Chu devised a sound plan that none of his ministers could match, he appeared at court looking troubled. When Marquis Wu of Wei devised a sound plan in consultation with his ministers that none of them could match, he appeared at court looking pleased. The pleased man took pride in his strengths; the troubled man worried about his shortcomings. …

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:

受人人臣當直道以事君君臣各盡其道
則天下事無不治矣其論禮樂也則曰禮
樂必本於德三代之德盛故禮樂達於天
下後世德不如古禮樂但有其具而無其

translation_en:
…This is why Marquis Wu fell short of King Zhuang of Chu. Thus a ruler should humble his mind to receive counsel from others, and a minister should serve his ruler with uprightness. When ruler and ministers each fulfill their proper way, no affairs under Heaven will remain disordered.” On rites and music, he said: “Rites and music must be rooted in virtue. The virtue of the Three Dynasties flourished, and therefore rites and music reached throughout the realm. In later ages, virtue has fallen short of antiquity: rites and music retain only their outward apparatus, without their substance. How, then, can rites and music flourish?” He also said: “Recently I ordered ancient musical instruments to be made, intending to distribute them to schools throughout the realm for sacrifices to Confucius. Yet the verses of ancient music were harmonious and correct, while the lyrics of later ages are licentious and extravagant. The pitch standards of antiquity accorded with the natural numerical patterns of Heaven and Earth; those of later ages arose from the private contrivances of human ingenuity. The seasons of Heaven and the vital influences of Earth are not properly examined, and human voices and instrumental sounds are not brought into accord. Thus, even if ancient verses and the prescribed configurations of ancient instruments are used, they will still clash rather than harmonize, encroaching upon one another without proper order. Human performance and music stand wholly apart; seeking thereby to move Heaven and Earth and stir ghosts and spirits—is this not difficult? But these practices have persisted for so long that remedying them is exceedingly difficult. Now we should devote careful thought to this matter, bring the music to completion, and distribute it for practice, so that we may recover the intentions of the ancients.”
Such are the principal things that I have heard from my teachers and friends. Instances of this kind cannot all be recounted. Alas! Our sagely founding emperor occupied the throne for more than thirty years. His admirable words and good deeds, his counsels and instructions, his achievements and glorious accomplishments were vast…

translation_en:
…vast and great indeed! Although at the time there were daily chronicles to record these things and court historians to continue the record, and later the Veritable Records compiled them and the Book of the Five Human Relationships brought them to light, I fear there may still be cause to lament that they have not been fully preserved. Yet who am I, in my ignorance, to expound and extol even one ten-thousandth of them? Allow me also to speak of his writings and institutions. The Ancestral Instructions of the August Ming established models for his descendants; the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements admonished his officials and people. Works such as the Comprehensive Instructions for Guiding the World and the commentary on the “Great Plan” likewise transmitted instruction to both high and low. These are all imperially authored canons of enduring authority. Other works, such as the Precious Instructions, the Statutes and Pronouncements, the Official Responsibilities, and the Collected Rituals, were composed and arranged by Confucian officials acting under imperial command.

Ah! Among the ancients there were surely those who understood and cherished the “Great Plan” and “Against Idleness”; the Sagely Founder, however, truly embodied them in his person and mind. Among the ancients there were surely those who wished to imitate and implement the six canons of the Offices of Zhou but fell short; the Sagely Founder judiciously put them into practice in his own age. What he delighted in reading during intervals between the myriad affairs of state was precisely what he implemented when administering government and striving for good order. Was it merely that the imperially authored works and those compiled at his command complemented these ancient texts? If this is so, then…

text:
執事之所謂存之于
聖心發之而為大訓行之而為大典有不專在
乎言語文字間者其無乃亦此之謂乎管
見如斯未知是否惟進而教之
第二問
霍韜
同考試官給事中高批五策通達古今
時宜資深經傳左右逢原且能一洗迂腐故
習而不區區於章句之末况前二塲精粹典
雅真奇傑之才醇正之學羣博之英俊也是
篇獨主君臣交修立說議論英發才氣沛乎
有不可遏者故特錄之惜其不能盡錄也
同考試官檢討孫批事問及災異古今
人不易於言顧人臣愛
君體
國所不能已雲漢板之諸詩人盖深致念焉易房經生能歷
歷引之為對非平日旁及諸經者有是乎餘
策自可錄錄此欲專經者知所勵心矣

執事之所謂在心之于
聖心發之而為大訓行之而為大典有不專在
乎言語文字間者其無乃亦此之謂乎譬
見如斯未知是否惟進而教之
第二問
霍韜
同考試給事中高　批〔五策通達古今〕
時宜資深經傳左右逢原且能一洗迂腐敢
習而不區區於章句之末况前二塲精粹典
雅真奇傑之才醇正之學辯博之英俊也是
===
篇獨主君臣交修立說議論英發有氣沛乎
有不可過者故特録之惜其不能盡録也
同考試官檢討孫　批〔事問及災異古今〕
人不易於言顧人臣愛
君體
國所不能已雲漢板之諸詩人盖深致念焉易房經生能歷
歷引之為對非平日究旁及諸經者有是乎餘
策自可録録此故專經者知所勵心矣
punctuated:
執事之所謂存之于聖心，發之而為大訓，行之而為大典，有不專在乎言語文字間者，其無乃亦此之謂乎？管見如斯，未知是否，惟進而教之。

第二問
霍韜

同考試官給事中高批：五策通達古今時宜，資深經傳，左右逢原，且能一洗迂腐故習，而不區區於章句之末。况前二塲精粹典雅，真奇傑之才、醇正之學、羣博之英俊也。是篇獨主君臣交修立說，議論英發，才氣沛乎有不可遏者，故特錄之。惜其不能盡錄也。

同考試官檢討孫批：事問及災異，古今人不易於言。顧人臣愛君體國，所不能已。《雲漢》《板》之諸詩，人盖深致念焉。易房經生能歷歷引之為對，非平日旁及諸經者有是乎？餘策自可錄，錄此欲專經者知所勵心矣。
translation_en:
…What you, sir, describe as being preserved in the sagely mind, expressed as great admonitions, and put into practice as great institutions—something not confined to speech and writing—surely refers to this as well? Such is my limited understanding. I do not know whether it is correct; I ask you to offer further instruction.

Second Policy Question
Huo Tao

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Supervising Secretary: The five policy essays display a thorough understanding of past and present and of what suits the needs of the time. Deeply grounded in the classics and their commentaries, they draw upon their sources at every turn. They also sweep away stale, pedantic habits, without becoming preoccupied with the minutiae of textual interpretation. Moreover, his work in the first two sessions is refined and classically elegant. Truly, he possesses exceptional talent and sound, orthodox learning, and is outstanding among men of broad scholarship. This essay alone builds its argument around the mutual cultivation of ruler and ministers. Its reasoning is brilliant, and its intellectual vigor surges irrepressibly. We have therefore selected it for inclusion. It is regrettable that we cannot include them all.

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Examining Editor: The question touches upon calamities and anomalies, matters that people past and present have found difficult to discuss. Yet a minister’s love for his ruler and concern for the state make it impossible to remain silent. In such poems as “The Milky Way” (Yunhan) and “Perversity” (Ban), the poets gave these matters profound consideration. This candidate in the Book of Changes examination section can cite them one by one in his response. Could anyone do this without regularly extending his studies to the other classics? His other policy essays are certainly worthy of inclusion. We include this one to show those who specialize in a single classic where to direct their efforts.

text:
同考試官編修景批五策出入經史才
氣渾厚體裁古雅識見不凡而此篇更佳持
錄之用示天下浮靡之習當為之一變
同考試官編修李批此卷初二試已知
其不凡五策貫串經史餘數千言若有不窮
其說者是篇溫醇典則忠愛之誠溢於言外
尤見學識主司得之良以自慶春闈首選無
以易子矣
考試官學士毛批灾異之降昔人以為
===
天心仁愛人君觀此策又可見斯人愛
君之深若子之於父母然言不盡而意有餘也况他篇皆迥出
人右天下之士顧不當讓之先乎
考試官大學士梁批五策貫串古今出入
經史至論人論事論治道處皆確然若有所
見且詞意周悉忠厚不失諷諫之體觀此一
對亦足以稍知其大畧矣况前二場皆詳整
明暢他日對揚
□□其洋洋為董賈之對者乎

translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Jing, Hanlin Academy Compiler: The five policy essays range through the classics and histories. Their literary force is full and substantial, their form classically elegant, and their discernment exceptional; this essay is finer still. It is selected for inclusion [?] to show the realm, so that the prevailing taste for superficial ornament may thereby be transformed.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Hanlin Academy Compiler: From the first and second sessions, this examination script was already recognizable as extraordinary. The five policy essays weave together the classics and histories; over several thousand further words [?], the writer seems to have inexhaustible arguments. This essay is measured, rich, and exemplary. Sincere loyalty and affection for the ruler overflow beyond its words, revealing his learning and judgment especially clearly. We examiners truly congratulate ourselves on having found him. As first choice in the Metropolitan Examination, you have no equal.

Comment by Examiner Mao, Hanlin Academician: When calamities and anomalies descended, men of old took them to signify Heaven’s benevolent love for the ruler. Reading this policy essay, one can also see the depth of this man’s love for his sovereign, like that of a child for his parents: his words cannot express it fully, and his meaning extends beyond them. Moreover, his other essays all far surpass those of others. Should not the scholars of the realm yield first place to him?

Comment by Examiner Liang, Grand Secretary: The five policy essays connect past and present and range through the classics and histories. Wherever they discuss people, events, or the way of government, their judgments are firm, as though grounded in clear insight. Their language and meaning are comprehensive, loyal, and generous, preserving the proper manner of indirect remonstrance. Reading this single response is enough to gain some sense of the broad scope of his abilities. Moreover, his work in the preceding two sessions was thorough, orderly, clear, and fluent. When in days to come he responds to and extols □□ [two illegible characters], will his expansive response not be like those of Dong and Jia?

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
對夫災變可懼也而亦可以為喜也知其
所以為可懼而盡夫修弭之道焉則變災
為祥之幾在於我而喜亦在乎其中矣昔
楚莊王見天無妖異則禱于山川以為天
且忘我而董仲舒亦以為天心仁愛人君
故欲以此止其亂豈非皆有見於是乎然
則明問所謂自古賢聖之君不以天無災
異為可喜而惟以德政未修為可懼者其
意亦猶是而已愚嘗求之詩雲漢之詩古
===
之人君之所以畏天者也如曰昊天上帝
則不我遺曰昊天上帝寧俾我遯其憂危
何如也然又必至於靡神而不舉靡人而
不周與庶正而共鞠也與冢宰而共疚也
夫豈泄泄然而無所事哉大雅板之詩古
之人臣之所以畏天者也如曰敬天之怒
無敢戲豫敬天之渝無敢馳驅其兢惕何
如也然又必欲其君致謹於价人大師之
藩垣留意於大宗大邦之屏翰與夫辭之

所以爲可懼而盡夫修弭之道焉則變災
爲祥之幾在於我而喜亦在乎其中矣昔

且忘我而董仲舒亦以爲天心仁愛人君
故欲以此止其亂豈非皆有見於是乎然
則明聞所謂自古賢聖之君不以天無災
異爲可喜而惟以德政未修爲可懼者其
意亦猶是而已愚嘗求之詩雲漢之詩古
===
之人君之所以畏天者也如曰昊天上帝
則不我遺曰昊天上帝寧俾我遯其憂危
何如也然又必至於靡神而不舉靡人而
不周與庶正而共鞠也與冢宰而共疚也
夫豈泄泄然而無所事哉大雅板之詩古
之人臣之所以畏天者也如曰敬天之怒
無敢戲豫敬天之渝無敢馳驅其兢惕何
如也然又必欲其君致謹於价人大師之
藩垣留意於大宗大邦之屏翰與夫辭之
punctuated: 對：夫災變可懼也，而亦可以為喜也。知其所以為可懼，而盡夫修弭之道焉，則變災為祥之幾在於我，而喜亦在乎其中矣。昔楚莊王見天無妖異，則禱于山川，以為天且忘我；而董仲舒亦以為天心仁愛人君，故欲以此止其亂。豈非皆有見於是乎？然則明問所謂自古賢聖之君不以天無災異為可喜，而惟以德政未修為可懼者，其意亦猶是而已。愚嘗求之《詩》。《雲漢》之詩，古之人君之所以畏天者也。如曰：「昊天上帝，則不我遺。」曰：「昊天上帝，寧俾我遯。」其憂危何如也！然又必至於靡神而不舉，靡人而不周，與庶正而共鞠也，與冢宰而共疚也，夫豈泄泄然而無所事哉？《大雅》〈板〉之詩，古之人臣之所以畏天者也。如曰：「敬天之怒，無敢戲豫；敬天之渝，無敢馳驅。」其兢惕何如也！然又必欲其君致謹於价人大師之藩垣，留意於大宗大邦之屏翰，與夫辭之
translation_en:
Reply: Calamities and prodigies are indeed to be feared, yet they may also be cause for joy. If we understand why they are fearful and fully pursue the means of reforming our conduct and averting them, the opportunity to turn calamity into auspicious fortune lies within our own power, and therein lies cause for joy. Formerly, when King Zhuang of Chu saw that Heaven sent no ominous anomalies, he prayed to the mountains and rivers, believing that Heaven was about to forget him. Dong Zhongshu likewise held that Heaven benevolently loves the ruler and therefore seeks through these signs to halt his misrule. Did they not both perceive this principle? Thus, your discerning question states that the worthy and sage rulers of antiquity did not rejoice because Heaven sent no calamities or anomalies, but feared only that their virtue and governance remained uncultivated. Its meaning is simply this same principle.

I have sought confirmation of this in the Book of Odes. The ode “The Milky Way” (Yunhan) shows how rulers of antiquity stood in awe of Heaven. It says, for example, “Vast Heaven, Sovereign on High, will not spare me,” and “Vast Heaven, Sovereign on High, would you make me flee?” How profound their anxiety and sense of peril! Yet they also went so far as to leave no spirit without sacrifice and no person without care, sharing the distress of the various chief officials and the suffering of the Grand Steward. How could they have remained idle and done nothing?

The ode “Perversity” (Ban), in the Greater Odes, shows how ministers of antiquity stood in awe of Heaven. It says, for example, “Revere Heaven’s wrath; dare not indulge in play and pleasure. Revere Heaven’s changing course; dare not gallop recklessly about.” How vigilant and apprehensive they were! Yet they also insisted that their ruler attend carefully to the great men and the multitudes who constituted his protective walls, and give thought to the great lineages and great states that served as his shields and supports, and also, as for his words …

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
欲其輯也民之欲其洽也亦豈但懽懽然
而不事其事哉夫周之君臣其心于憂畏
也如此而後世之諱過者乃至於指旱嘆
以為乾封之祥其獻諛者乃復誣水旱以
為常數不足畏嗚呼其亦獨何心哉請試
為執事誦所聞昔堯湯之時非無洪水大
旱之災也然堯則曰洚水警予也其臣則
過家不入惟荒度土功也湯則以六事自
責也其臣則咸有一德一夫不獲若撻于
===
市也然則洪水大旱之災其何足以為聖
治之害也哉太戊武丁之時亦非無桑穀
雊雉之異也然二君既克自抑畏以修德
於上伊陟甘盤之為臣又皆克厭天心以
輔治於下然則桑穀雉雊之妖又何足以
勝其畏天之德也哉乃若漢之文景宋之
仁宗皆後世守成之令主考其當時災異
尤為眾多然文景則躬修玄默恭儉愛民
羣臣則悃幅無華類多長者仁宗在位最

punctuated: 欲其輯也，民之欲其洽也，亦豈但懽懽然而不事其事哉？夫周之君臣，其心于憂畏也如此，而後世之諱過者，乃至於指旱嘆以為乾封之祥；其獻諛者，乃復誣水旱以為常數不足畏。嗚呼！其亦獨何心哉？請試為執事誦所聞。昔堯湯之時，非無洪水大旱之災也，然堯則曰：「洚水警予也。」其臣則過家不入，惟荒度土功也。湯則以六事自責也，其臣則咸有一德，一夫不獲，若撻于市也。然則洪水大旱之災，其何足以為聖治之害也哉？太戊武丁之時，亦非無桑穀雊雉之異也，然二君既克自抑畏，以修德於上，伊陟甘盤之為臣，又皆克厭天心，以輔治於下。然則桑穀雉雊之妖，又何足以勝其畏天之德也哉？乃若漢之文景、宋之仁宗，皆後世守成之令主。考其當時，災異尤為眾多，然文景則躬修玄默，恭儉愛民；羣臣則悃幅無華，類多長者。仁宗在位最
translation_en:
…wishing their words to be harmonious and their people to live in concord—could they merely have rejoiced without attending to their duties? Such was the anxious and reverent disposition of the rulers and ministers of Zhou. Yet those in later ages who concealed faults went so far as to point to drought [?] as an auspicious sign for the Feng sacrifice (qianfeng) [?]; those who offered flattery even falsely claimed that floods and droughts were ordinary occurrences that need not be feared. Alas! What could have been in their hearts? Allow me to recount for you what I have heard.

In the days of Yao and Tang, there were indeed disasters of great floods and severe drought. Yet Yao said, “The floodwaters warn me.” His minister passed his own home without entering, devoting himself to planning the great works of flood control. Tang reproached himself on six counts. His minister possessed undivided virtue: if even one person failed to find his proper place, he felt as though he himself were being flogged in the marketplace. How, then, could disasters of flood and drought have harmed their sagely government?

In the days of Taiwu and Wuding, there were likewise anomalies involving a mulberry and a paper mulberry, and a crowing pheasant. Yet both rulers could humble themselves in reverent fear and cultivate virtue above, while their ministers Yi Zhi and Gan Pan could satisfy Heaven’s heart and assist their government below. How, then, could the ominous mulberry trees and crowing pheasant have prevailed over their virtue of revering Heaven?

As for Emperors Wen and Jing of Han and Emperor Renzong of Song, all were excellent rulers of later ages who preserved their inherited achievements. Examination of their times shows that disasters and anomalies were especially numerous. Yet Wen and Jing personally cultivated profound stillness, practiced reverence and frugality, and cherished the people. Their ministers were sincere and unadorned [?], and most were men of mature integrity. Renzong’s reign was the longest…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
久既以深仁厚澤結天下而一時賢俊更
入迭出又能以通經學古共濟時艱是故
雖各有其異而竟無其應豈非天實佑之
而致然哉恭惟
皇上道高德厚治教休明近者遇此災變又不
諉罪臣下且大行寬
詔於天下欲使臣民各得其所此即堯湯求
治之心亦太戊武丁責己之心也他日致
治之美與
===
福德壽考之盛尚當躋文景仁宗之上而遠
過之一時水旱凶荒螟蝗盜賊之災變亦
自將消除泯滅而無復有後艱者矣又何
足以深勞吾大臣之過慮也哉然而執事
發策下教承學則曰吾大小臣工奉行德
政有所未盡而致然也則曰此吾臣子之
所以祗承
德意慚懼而不能自已者也則曰欲重為
上詳陳之冀萬一涓埃之報而未能也懃懃不

Recently, when confronted with these calamities and anomalies, you did not shift the blame onto your ministers. This is precisely the determination of Yao and Tang to achieve good government, and likewise the determination of Taiwu and Wuding to hold themselves accountable. In days to come, the excellence of your government and the abundance of your blessings, virtue, and longevity will surely rise above those of Emperors Wen and Jing and Emperor Renzong, surpassing them by far. The present calamities of floods and droughts, crop failures and famine, caterpillars and locusts, and banditry will also naturally disappear and be eradicated, leaving no further troubles. …without ceasing, you further look to the examination candidates to set forth fully their loyal sentiments, intending to draw upon these to convey their views to His Majesty. Ah! With such intentions, are you not an example of what is meant by attributing good to the ruler and taking fault upon oneself? Are you not an example of the saying that a minister who can follow what is good can make his ruler good, and a minister who can heed remonstrance can remonstrate with his ruler? Dull-witted though I am, how could I fail to revere and admire your lofty sense of duty? Allow me, for the moment, to address you on the single matter of investigating the people's sufferings.
When Heaven brought forth the multitude of people, they could not sustain themselves unaided, so it necessarily brought forth a great sovereign to instruct and nurture them. Nor can the ruler, in governing all under Heaven, manage everything alone: he must entrust great ministers with assisting him in government. If ruler and ministers each discharge their responsibilities, bringing good order to all under Heaven and aiding its people, August Heaven's favor and protection will naturally endure without decline. If one seeks a way to avert calamities and anomalies, what could surpass this? Yet while the people's security or distress is experienced below, the power that determines it lies above. Without lightening labor services and reducing taxation, they cannot be brought security; without selecting and employing conscientious and benevolent officials, they cannot be brought security. Why, then, in recent years have the demands that the responsible officials impose upon those below increased daily, while the common people, rushing about to furnish supplies to their superiors, have grown daily more distressed? Their strength exhausted, they cannot bear the labor services; their resources depleted, they cannot meet the demands. Unless they turn to banditry, they are left to become corpses of the starved. As for bringing them security…

Those who plan well for the state are those who cultivate themselves within the family; those who understand the present are those thoroughly versed in antiquity. For the Way is one, and nothing more. If a scholar cultivates himself within the family, he will assuredly be loyal when he goes forth to serve his sovereign. If through study he becomes thoroughly versed in antiquity, he will assuredly show understanding when applying his learning to current affairs. This is simply what is meant by taking what one has learned and putting it into practice. In issuing this policy question, you have drawn together various earlier thinkers’ discussions of government and condescended to consult us students. 可行於賢愚同滯之朝此宣公之所以酌

明於政體而存其大或審乎事要而急所

To ensure that metropolitan graduates (jinshi) read closely and learn to write correctly, the crucial measure lies in the examination questions set by the responsible officials. As for the writings of the various masters, only those that support the Classics and accord with the Way should be selected: this was what Zhang Zhibai told Emperor Zhenzong. To ensure that scholar-officials esteem prefectural appointments and take pleasure in remaining in office, the foundation lies in the court’s treatment, rewards, and encouragement of them. This was why the Marquis of Wu (Zhuge Liang) favored stern measures and imposed the authority of law. The argument for long tenure could be put into practice in an age when prefects received accelerated promotion, but not at a court where worthy and foolish alike languished without advancement. This was why Duke Xuan (Lu Zhi) weighed ancient and contemporary practice and adopted a balanced course.

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Supervising Secretary: Learning for service in the world is not to be judged by literary accomplishment alone. This essay sets out current affairs point by point, as though its proposals had long been settled. Moreover, its plans are apt and well considered, every one demonstrably practicable. What is called understanding the times and responding effectively to change finds confirmation in you [?].
Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Examining Editor: When people discuss affairs, they say, “A scholar’s talk,” meaning merely that it is impractical; or “Talk from books,” meaning merely that it is useless. Yet is it the person who is useless, or the books [?]? Is not a policy answer such as this written by a scholar and drawn from his books? Yet it examines antiquity to devise plans for the present, and there seems to be nothing in it that cannot be put into practice. I imagine that he has long devoted his mind to worldly affairs. This essay alone draws on established views of the ancients while reaching judgments of its own. Neither pedantic nor rigid, its proposals are demonstrably practicable. 之宜蓋即古人論今事之當然不若求古
道于已然之意也抑嘗聞諸東萊呂氏云
觀其處今事之跡則知其談古道之謬談
古道之謬則其處今事之跡也可知矣若
愚輩者執事復何取焉雖然言及之而不
言隱也請試言之執事試聽之水利之制
===
嘗於禹貢而有得乎其槩矣禹貢一篇區
畫疆理之法至周而至備故隨山刊木濬
澮距川其跡導之法固可考而知也今則
水道湮而其利微矣自齊魯以北極目千
里皆膏腴之地霖雨於春則水無所洩而
一望瀰漫亢陽於夏則旱無所救而千里
枯槁民之嗷嗷於凍餒者恒以是也志于
經濟者獨不思所以興其利乎昔李冰在
蜀鑿離堆在兗西門豹在魏姜師度在易或
punctuated:
之可行，則法立而人可以守，事濟而後可以持循矣。執事以水利、馬政、屯田、鹽法下詢末學，且欲考古人已試之法，而推以當今之宜，盖即古人論今事之當然，不若求古道于已然之意也。抑嘗聞諸東萊吕氏云：「觀其處今事之疎，則知其談古道之謬；談古道之謬，則其處今事之疎也可知矣。」若愚輩者，執事復何取焉？雖然，言及之而不言，隱也。請試言之，執事試聽之。

水利之制，嘗於《禹貢》而有得乎其槩矣。《禹貢》一篇，區畫疆理之法，至周而至備。故隨山刋木，濬澮距川，其疏導之法，固可考而知也。今則水道湮而其利微矣。自齊魯以北，極目千里，皆膏腴之地。霖雨於春，則水無所洩，而一望瀰漫；亢陽於夏，則旱無所救，而千里枯槁。民之嗷嗷於凍餒者，恒以是也。志于經濟者，獨不思所以興其利乎？昔李氷在蜀，薛冑在兖，西門豹在魏，姜師度在易，或
translation_en:
…what can be put into practice, then the laws established can be observed by the people, and successful undertakings can thereafter be maintained. You, sir, have deigned to question this humble student about water management, horse administration, military agricultural colonies, and the salt regulations. You also wish to examine methods already tested by the ancients and adapt them to present needs. This accords with the ancients’ meaning: discussing what ought to be done in present affairs is less useful than seeking the ancient Way in what has actually been accomplished. Yet I have heard Master Lü of Donglai say: “Observe how ineptly someone handles present affairs, and you will know how mistaken his discussions of the ancient Way are; from the errors in his discussions of the ancient Way, his ineptitude in handling present affairs can likewise be known.” What, then, could you find of value in ignorant people such as myself? Nevertheless, to remain silent when a subject has been raised is to conceal what one knows. Allow me to attempt an explanation, and may you, sir, hear it.

As for water management, I have gained some understanding of its broad outlines from the Tribute of Yu. The methods of territorial division and boundary demarcation set out in that chapter reached their fullest development under the Zhou. Thus, following the mountains and clearing trees, dredging field channels to reach the rivers—their methods of drainage and channeling can certainly be understood through investigation. Today, however, the waterways are silted up, and their benefits have diminished. Northward from Qi and Lu, fertile land stretches as far as the eye can see, for a thousand li. When prolonged rains fall in spring, the water has nowhere to drain, and flooding extends across the entire view. When fierce sunshine prevails in summer, there is no relief from drought, and the land withers for a thousand li. This is constantly why the people cry out in cold and hunger. Can those devoted to ordering the world and aiding the people fail to consider how to develop these benefits? In former times, Li Bing served in Shu, Xue Zhou in Yan, Ximen Bao in Wei, and Jiang Shidu in Yi; some…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
鑿渠或築陂皆灌田數十萬頃民至今稱
之司民牧者倣其法而行之夫豈不可乎
牧馬之制嘗於簡牒而有得乎其畧矣漢
書曰班氏居塞則致馬數千羣桃橋居塞
則致馬千匹其牧養之制亦可考而知也
今則馬政弛而其法隳矣軍行無馬有徒
手搏虎之憂倉卒支吾行鬻爵買馬之令
兵之每每孱弱者凡以是也志於用世者
寧不思所以去其弊乎昔衛文公以秉心
===
塞淵而致駔牝之三千張萬歲以盡職隴
右而致七十萬匹之盛其存國於既亡濟
用於當世載在史冊至于今誦之司國計
者倣其法而行之又豈不可乎屯田之興
久矣孫氏曰千里饋糧士有饑色樵蘇後
爨師不宿飽惟屯田內有亡費之利外有
守禦之備其在今日蓋尤所不可緩者奈
何文具雖存廢格如故士卒役于將校之
私門田里荒于豪右之吞併望其有升斗

塞淵而致騋牝之三千張萬歲以盡職隴
右而致七十萬匹之盛其存國於既亡濟
用於當世載在史冊至于今誦之司國計
者倣其法而行之又豈不可乎屯田之興
久矣孫氏曰千里饋糧士有饑色樵蘇後
爨師不宿飽惟屯田內有亡費之利外有
守禦之備其在今日蓋尤所不可緩者奈
何文具雖存廢格如故士卒役于將校之
私門田里荒于豪右之吞併望其有升斗
punctuated:
鑿渠，或築陂，皆灌田數十萬頃，民至今稱之。司民牧者倣其法而行之，夫豈不可乎？
牧馬之制，嘗於簡牒而有得乎其畧矣。《漢書》曰：「班氏居塞，則致馬數千羣；桃橋居塞，則致馬千匹。」其牧養之制，亦可考而知也。今則馬政弛而其法隳矣。軍行無馬，有徒手搏虎之憂；倉卒支吾，行鬻爵買馬之令。兵之每每孱弱者，凡以是也。志於用世者，寧不思所以去其弊乎？昔衛文公以秉心塞淵，而致駔牝之三千；張萬歲以盡職隴右，而致七十萬匹之盛。其存國於既亡，濟用於當世，載在史冊，至于今誦之。司國計者倣其法而行之，又豈不可乎？
屯田之興久矣。孫氏曰：「千里饋糧，士有饑色；樵蘇後爨，師不宿飽。」惟屯田，內有亡費之利，外有守禦之備。其在今日，蓋尤所不可緩者。奈何文具雖存，廢格如故？士卒役于將校之私門，田里荒于豪右之吞併，望其有升斗
translation_en:
…dug canals or built reservoirs, each irrigating several hundred thousand qing of farmland; the people praise them to this day. Could those charged with governing and tending the people not follow their methods and put them into practice?
As for the system of horse pasturage, I have gained some understanding of its outlines from written records. The History of the Han states: “The Ban family lived on the frontier and accumulated several thousand herds of horses; Taoqiao [?] lived on the frontier and accumulated a thousand horses.” Their methods of pasturing and breeding can likewise be ascertained through study. Today, however, horse administration has grown lax and its regulations have fallen into disuse. Armies march without horses, facing dangers like those of fighting a tiger barehanded. Scrambling to cope in an emergency, the authorities issue orders to sell noble ranks to buy horses. This is why the troops are so often weak. How could those aspiring to serve the world fail to consider how to eliminate these abuses? In former times, Duke Wen of Wei, through his steadfast and profound resolve, acquired three thousand stallions and mares; Zhang Wansui, by diligently discharging his duties in Longyou, brought the herds to a flourishing total of seven hundred thousand horses. How they preserved a state after its destruction and supplied the needs of their age is recorded in the histories and recounted to this day. Could those responsible for state finances not likewise follow their methods and put them into practice?
Military agricultural colonies have long existed. Master Sun said: “When grain is transported a thousand li, the soldiers look hungry; when firewood and grass must be gathered before cooking, the army cannot count on a full meal from one night to the next.” Military agricultural colonies alone offer the domestic advantage of avoiding expenditure while providing for defense against external threats. Today, in particular, they surely cannot be delayed. Why, although the paperwork remains in place, are they still neglected and obstructed as before? Soldiers are put to work in the private households of their commanders, while farmland lies waste through annexation by powerful local families. To hope that they will yield even a sheng or a dou of grain…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
之入以佐軍國之需者寡矣盍亦講求其
法斷在必行亦必如趙充國之於湟中諸
葛亮之於渭濱大獲地利居民安堵屯田
其庶有實效乎鹽筴之興久矣范仲淹曰
既不能省費以節財則不免於用財而濟
事與其取之農孰若取之商朝廷立官以
禁之設法以斂之在今日亦所不可廢者
柰何成規徒在欺弊愈多上有所損於官
下有所傷於民欲其致山海之利為邊方
===
之助者難矣盍亦申嚴其禁靡所容私則
不必如桑孔之於漢劉晏之於唐而官民
兩利國用罔虧鹽法其庶無貽害乎是水
利也馬政也屯田也鹽法也四者皆今之
急務也執事又謂水利鹽法二者其補偏
捄弊之法成憲故在各有司存蓋不須别
有所建明惟在厲其所以害法之禁而其
法自行矣惟馬政與屯田之法非大有所
建明則不可豈以為當今之制既設有水

punctuated:
之入，以佐軍國之需者寡矣。盍亦講求其法，斷在必行，亦必如趙充國之於湟中、諸葛亮之於渭濱，大獲地利，居民安堵，屯田其庶有實效乎？

鹽筴之興久矣。范仲淹曰：「既不能省費以節財，則不免於用財而濟事。與其取之農，孰若取之商？」朝廷立官以禁之，設法以斂之，在今日亦所不可廢者。柰何成規徒在，欺弊愈多，上有所損於官，下有所傷於民，欲其致山海之利，為邊方之助者難矣。盍亦申嚴其禁，靡所容私，則不必如桑孔之於漢、劉晏之於唐，而官民兩利，國用罔虧，鹽法其庶無貽害乎？

是水利也，馬政也，屯田也，鹽法也，四者皆今之急務也。執事又謂水利、鹽法二者，其補偏捄弊之法，成憲故在，各有司存，蓋不須别有所建明，惟在厲其所以害法之禁，而其法自行矣。惟馬政與屯田之法，非大有所建明則不可。豈以為當今之制，既設有水
translation_en:
…yielding revenue to help meet military and state needs are few indeed. Why not investigate the methods and resolve that they must be put into practice? Surely, as with Zhao Chongguo in Huangzhong and Zhuge Liang on the banks of the Wei River, the land could be made highly productive and the inhabitants could live securely. Might military agricultural colonies then produce real results?

The salt monopoly has long been established. Fan Zhongyan said: “Since expenditure cannot be reduced to conserve resources, one cannot avoid using wealth to accomplish affairs. Rather than obtain it from farmers, would it not be better to obtain it from merchants?” The court appointed officials to enforce its prohibitions and established methods for collecting its revenues; these remain indispensable today. Yet why do the established regulations exist only in name, while fraud and abuses multiply, causing losses to the government above and harm to the people below? It is difficult under these circumstances to draw upon the wealth of mountains and seas to support the frontier. Why not enforce the prohibitions strictly, leaving no room for private interests? Then, without necessarily matching Sang and Kong under the Han or Liu Yan under the Tang, both officials and people could benefit, and state expenditure would be fully supplied. Might the salt administration then cease to cause harm?

Water management, horse administration, military agricultural colonies, and salt administration: these four are all urgent matters today. You further state that, for water management and salt administration, established statutes already provide methods for correcting imbalances and remedying abuses, and each has its responsible offices. There is therefore no need to propose additional measures; it is only necessary to enforce strictly the prohibitions against practices that undermine the regulations, and those regulations will operate of themselves. Only in horse administration and military agricultural colonies are substantial new proposals indispensable. Is this because you consider that, under the present system, there have already been appointed officials for water…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
利鹽法之官而漕運憲臣又兼掌修河通
漕之計夫既或治之矣而政不在於多門
也若牧馬之政則我
朝大學士丘文莊嘗別有建議謂再當於邦
畿之內設法牧養庶上不失
祖宗太僕之成法下有以寬民庶之困苦蓋其
意甚美而論建之說甚詳今欲舉而行之
夫孰云不可乎至若屯田之策元學士虞
集亦嘗言於勝國謂京師之東瀕海數千
===
里皆萑葦之場宜用浙人之法築堤捍水
為田廣種秔稻可歲收百萬餘石以濟國
用且可省漕運之費其議雖見沮於時
其後丞相脫脫用原議而舉行之果獲
利如集之言然亦既晚矣知言君子甚
惜之今若倣其法而行之又孰云不可乎
愚生學不足以知古才不足以適用姑以
所聞見求是正於明執事惟進而教之幸
甚

利、鹽法之官，而漕運憲臣又兼掌修河通漕之計，夫既或治之矣，而政不在於多門也。若牧馬之政，則我朝大學士丘文莊嘗別有建議，謂再當於邦畿之內設法牧養，庶上不失祖宗太僕之成法，下有以寬民庶之困苦。蓋其意甚美，而論建之說甚詳。今欲舉而行之，夫孰云不可乎？至若屯田之策，元學士虞集亦嘗言於勝國，謂京師之東瀕海數千里，皆萑葦之場，宜用浙人之法，築堤捍水，為田廣種秔稻，可歲收百萬餘石，以濟國用，且可省漕運之費。其議雖見沮於時，其後丞相脫脫用原議而舉行之，果獲利如集之言，然亦既晚矣。知言君子甚惜之。今若倣其法而行之，又孰云不可乎？

translation_en:
…officials for water conservancy and the salt administration, while the censorial official responsible for grain transport also oversees plans for repairing waterways and keeping grain shipments moving? Since someone already administers these matters, government should not proceed through multiple authorities. As for horse breeding, Qiu Wenzhuang, a Grand Secretary of our dynasty, once made a separate proposal, arguing that arrangements should again [?] be made to pasture and rear horses within the metropolitan region. This would preserve the ancestral emperors’ established regulations for the Court of the Imperial Stud while relieving the hardships of the common people. His intention was excellent, and his exposition of the proposal was very detailed. If we wished to put it into practice now, who could say it was impossible?
As for agricultural colonies, Yu Ji, an Academician of the Yuan, also once submitted a proposal to that former dynasty. He stated that the coastal land east of the capital, extending several thousand li, consisted entirely of reed beds. The methods used by the people of Zhejiang should be adopted: embankments could be built to keep out the water, and the land made into fields extensively planted with rice. These could yield more than a million shi of grain annually to meet state needs, while also saving the expense of grain transport. Although his proposal was obstructed at the time, the Chief Councilor Tuotuo later implemented the original proposal, and it indeed produced the benefits Yu Ji had predicted. By then, however, it was already too late. Gentlemen who could appreciate the soundness of his words deeply regretted this. If we were now to follow and implement his method, who could say it was impossible?
My learning, as an ignorant student, is insufficient to comprehend antiquity, and my abilities are insufficient for practical service. I have merely presented what I have heard and seen, seeking correction from you, my discerning examiner. If you would receive me and instruct me, I would be most fortunate.

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
盜之術亦多矣然孰若先其要哉不得其
要而能舉其術者未之有也其要何居亦
曰即盜賊之生以反求其所由生則其所
以弭之之要有不必廣詢而得之者矣愚
嘗慨夫饑寒不恤赤子弄兵龔遂既行而
渤海定贓吏誅求厥民怨叛賈琮一出而
交阯寧若近時盜賊之患謂不由此二端
乎固不可謂盡由此二端乎亦不可盖今
海內數年間沴氣為災殆無虛歲誠臣體
===
國曾幾何人方民之困於饑寒也率以安民
為迂闊而所以宣
上德者皆虛文及民之化為盜賊也則又視動
衆如尋常而所以處軍機者多僨事以包
容為盛德謂姑息為忠厚
國之紀綱黜陟為重賢者進矣不肖者退矣
然而不盡然也賦繁役重加之有司不職
如昔人所謂刺史無清行者此其人未必
皆去官也

punctuated:
盜之術亦多矣，然孰若先其要哉？不得其要而能舉其術者，未之有也。其要何居？亦曰：即盜賊之生，以反求其所由生，則其所以弭之之要，有不必廣詢而得之者矣。愚嘗慨夫饑寒不恤，赤子弄兵，龔遂既行而渤海定；贓吏誅求，厥民怨叛，賈琮一出而交阯寧。若近時盜賊之患，謂不由此二端乎？固不可。謂盡由此二端乎？亦不可。盖今海內數年間，沴氣為災，殆無虛歲。誠臣體國，曾幾何人？方民之困於饑寒也，率以安民為迂闊，而所以宣上德者皆虛文；及民之化為盜賊也，則又視動衆如尋常，而所以處軍機者多僨事。以包容為盛德，謂姑息為忠厚。

國之紀綱，黜陟為重。賢者進矣，不肖者退矣，然而不盡然也。賦繁役重，加之有司不職，如昔人所謂刺史無清行者，此其人未必皆去官也。
translation_en:
…the methods for suppressing banditry are indeed numerous, but which can compare with first attending to what is essential? There has never been anyone who could put such methods into effect without grasping their essentials. Where does the essential point lie? Simply this: examine the emergence of bandits and trace back the causes of their emergence. Then the essential means of suppressing them can be found without necessarily making extensive inquiries. I have often reflected with sorrow on how, when hunger and cold went unrelieved, the people, like innocent children, took up arms; once Gong Sui acted, Bohai was pacified. When corrupt officials made oppressive exactions, their people became resentful and rebelled; once Jia Cong went forth, Jiaozhi became tranquil. As for the recent scourge of banditry, can one say that it does not arise from these two causes? Certainly not. Can one say that it arises entirely from these two causes? Neither can one say that. In recent years throughout the realm, baleful forces have brought disasters, with scarcely a year free of them. How many sincere ministers have truly had the state's interests at heart [?]? While the people suffer hunger and cold, officials generally dismiss efforts to bring them peace as impractical, and everything they do to make the sovereign's virtue known amounts to empty formalities. Once the people turn into bandits, however, they treat mobilizing troops as an ordinary matter, and their handling of military affairs often brings failure. They regard indulgence as lofty virtue and call appeasement loyalty and generosity.

In maintaining the state's governing order, dismissal and promotion are weighty matters. The worthy are advanced and the unworthy removed—yet this is not invariably so. Taxes are numerous and labor obligations heavy; moreover, the responsible officials fail in their duties. Such men resemble those whom the ancients described as regional inspectors lacking integrity in their conduct. These men have by no means all been removed from office.

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
國之紀綱刑賞尤重有功者勸矣有罪者懲
矣然而不盡然也師老財匱固有統馭非
才如昔人所謂經畧使不得人者此其人
未必皆得罪也為氓之害切身而莫捄為
盜之利有餘而幸免由是奸頑桀黠奮臂
而前憃愚寡弱附勢而往盜賊之禍始有
不可勝言者矣嗚呼是孰使之然哉是則
致近時之盜固非一端而忽紀綱之重乃
其大者夫本其由既在於紀綱之或弛則
===
夫求所以弭之之術今而後安得不反前
之為而首以紀綱為務乎苟能振紀綱以
肅天下之心自將服盜賊以收天下之勢
何也紀綱既立百度皆舉也此固歐陽子
明賞罰去冗官用良吏之說而豈愚一人
之私言哉若夫秦觀所謂渠魁盡殺而弗
赦則足以奪奸雄之氣脅從汙染不治而
許其自新則足以安反側之心此其策誠
有過人者假使紀綱未立則廢格沮撓威

translation_en: In the state's governing order, punishments and rewards are especially important. Those who have rendered service are encouraged, and those who have committed offenses are chastened; yet this is not invariably so. When troops are worn out and resources exhausted, there are certainly commanders unequal to their duties—as people of earlier times put it, “the Military Commissioner is not the right man for the post.” Such men do not necessarily all receive punishment. The hardships of being an ordinary subject strike close to home, with no one to offer relief, while becoming a bandit brings ample profit and the chance of escaping punishment. Thus the wicked, obstinate, fierce, and cunning raise their arms and advance, while the foolish, ignorant, isolated, and weak follow their power. Only then do the calamities of banditry become impossible to recount fully. Alas! Who has brought this about? There is certainly more than one cause of the banditry of recent times, but neglect of the importance of the governing order is a principal one. Since its underlying cause lies in the occasional slackening of that order, how, in seeking a means to quell banditry from now on, can we fail to reverse our former conduct and make restoring that order our first concern? If we can invigorate it and thereby instill respect in the hearts of all under Heaven, we shall naturally subdue the bandits and regain command of affairs throughout the realm. Why? Once the governing order is established, all institutions function properly. This is precisely Master Ouyang's teaching: make rewards and punishments clear, eliminate superfluous officials, and employ good administrators. How could it be merely my own humble, private opinion? As for Qin Guan's statement that executing all the ringleaders without pardon would suffice to break the spirit of the wicked and ambitious, while refraining from prosecuting those coerced into joining and tainted by association, and allowing them to reform themselves, would suffice to set uneasy hearts at rest—this policy truly surpasses others. But if the governing order has not yet been established, there will be failures of implementation and obstruction, and authority…

text:
固不振惠亦何施由是言之弭盜賊之術
誠莫要乎惟紀綱之修者盖
朝廷之明斷罔愆則天下之觀望頓異民心
向善盜賊自消又何假於别設科目以收
遺才使奸雄無徒哉此則子瞻一時之見
愚未敢以為策之善也吾能制之奸雄自
服無以制之則授之官爵適資其亂也嗚
呼莫先紀綱信其然矣故曰善計天下者

punctuated: 固不振，惠亦何施？由是言之，弭盜賊之術，誠莫要乎惟紀綱之修者。盖朝廷之明斷罔愆，則天下之觀望頓異，民心向善，盜賊自消，又何假於别設科目以收遺才，使奸雄無徒哉？此則子瞻一時之見，愚未敢以為策之善也。吾能制之，奸雄自服；無以制之，則授之官爵，適資其亂也。嗚呼！莫先紀綱，信其然矣。故曰：善計天下者，視其紀綱之存，而治可知也。方今聖政維新，盜賊且平，民困且甦，若無足慮者。然往事明徵，自可為將来之戒，而狂言太早，亦不失為先事之圖也。惟執事舉而獻之九重，謀之卿士，天下幸甚。
translation_en:
…authority certainly cannot be asserted; how, then, can benevolence be bestowed? From this we may say that, among the means of suppressing banditry, nothing is more essential than restoring the governing order and discipline. For if the court’s discerning decisions are without error, expectations throughout the realm will immediately change. The people’s hearts will turn toward goodness, and banditry will disappear of itself. What need would there be to establish a separate examination category to recruit overlooked talent, so that ambitious evildoers have no followers? This was merely Zizhan’s view at a particular moment; I dare not regard it as a sound policy. If we can keep such men under control, they will submit of themselves. If we have no means of controlling them, granting them offices and ranks will only furnish resources for their disorder. Alas! Nothing takes precedence over governing order and discipline: this is indeed true. Thus I say: those who deliberate well on the affairs of the realm examine whether its governing order and discipline remain intact, and from this its state of governance can be known.
At present, sagely government is being renewed; banditry is nearing pacification, and the people are beginning to recover from their hardships. There seems to be nothing sufficient to cause concern. Yet the clear lessons of past events can serve as warnings for the future; and although these rash words may come too early, they may still constitute a plan made before trouble arises. I ask only that you take up these proposals and present them to the Emperor within his ninefold palace, and deliberate upon them with the high ministers and officers. This would be a great blessing for the realm.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the jiaxu year of the Zhengde reign [1514], the Ministry of Rites held the Metropolitan Examination for scholars from throughout the realm. His Majesty ordered senior ministers distinguished in literary learning to serve as Examiners, and this appointment undeservedly extended to me, your servant Cheng. Once the command had been issued, on the xinchou day of that month we took leave of His Majesty and entered the examination compound. On the third day, guimao, we held the first session; on bingwu, the second; and on jiyou, the final session. In accordance with the prescribed quota, we selected four hundred men. We also had their names and compositions engraved for printing as the Record of the Metropolitan Examination, to submit it humbly for His Majesty’s perusal and make it known throughout the realm. translation_en:
…His Majesty’s benevolent intentions, none daring to slacken. After twenty days of such effort, the work was completed. We reverently reflect that, when Taizu founded our dynasty, he established institutions for the age and instituted the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) examination to receive the outstanding men of the realm. His sagely sons and divine grandsons have maintained it unchanged for what is now a hundred and fifty years. Because selection has been exacting, its success in obtaining worthy men has been exceptional.
Ruler and ministers have been united in virtue, shared by those above and below; in the grandeur of their achievements, successive generations have matched one another. Ah! Is this why metropolitan graduates are esteemed in our age? At the outset they are selected through their words, but in the end they truly fulfill the state’s expectations of outstanding men. How could the world fail to esteem them? Thus we may understand that it is not their literary accomplishments that are esteemed. I have sought examples in earlier dynasties, such as Lu Zhi of the Tang and Han Qi of the Song…

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
聖子神孫守爲成憲後先豪傑背
此焉出豈不由
聖祖詒謀之遠而致然哉抑嘗聞
聖祖有言
朕每觀天象自洪武初有黑氣凝
於奎壁間奎壁乃文章之府
心甚異之今年春暮其間黑
===
氣始消文運自此當興矣時
二十七年九月也當是時左
右侍臣聞者盖無不拜稽稱
慶烏乎是豈非儒道之大幸
而亦豈非科目復行慶延百
世之嘉兆也哉正德九年春
正月禮部尚書臣劉春侍郎

His sagely sons and divine grandsons maintained this as an established institution, and outstanding men of successive generations emerged through it [?]. Was this not the result of the far-reaching plans bequeathed by the Sagely Ancestor? Moreover, I have heard that the Sagely Ancestor once said: “Whenever I observed the celestial phenomena, from the beginning of the Hongwu reign, there was a dark vapor gathered between Kui and Bi. Kui and Bi are the celestial repositories of literary accomplishment, so I found this profoundly strange. In late spring this year, the dark vapor between them finally began to dissipate. From this time onward, literary fortunes should flourish.” This was in the ninth month of the twenty-seventh year of Hongwu. At that time, all the attendant ministers who heard these words bowed, knocked their heads to the ground, and offered congratulations. Ah! Was this not a great blessing for the Confucian Way, and also an auspicious portent that the resumption of the examinations would bring blessings extending through a hundred generations?

title: 正德九年會試錄
text:
范仲淹皆其人也或當艱難
之初勢雖危疑言必剴切或
定策兩朝德望盖世或感激
論國家事奮不顧身為天下
第一流人物至今雖新學小
生亦能誦其言悚然知所敬
慕嗚呼盛矣惟我
===
皇明以儒術造就宇內人才士方
游學校則已知宗孔孟務道
德盖不專以文藝相高也乃
至於成進士身為世用人皆
以古豪傑望我若終無所建
立則何以異於凡民哉固宜
每科必有巍然大才建功樹

…Fan Zhongyan was also among such men. Some, at the onset of adversity, spoke with unfailing frankness and pertinence, even amid peril and uncertainty; some settled plans for the succession in two reigns, their virtue and prestige unsurpassed in their age; some spoke passionately on affairs of state, exerting themselves without regard for their own safety. They were men of the very first rank in the realm. Even today, young beginners in learning can recite their words and feel a profound sense of reverence and admiration. Ah, how splendid!
Our august Ming dynasty cultivates talent throughout the realm through Confucian learning. While scholars are still studying in the schools, they already know to take Confucius and Mencius as their masters and to devote themselves to the Way and virtue; they do not seek to outdo one another solely in literary accomplishment. Once they become metropolitan graduates (jinshi) and enter the service of the age, each must reflect: “Everyone expects me to measure up to the great men of antiquity.
